I wish to make a slight correction in answer to a question asked by the hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) about a week ago. The question was as follows:
1.	Has the Department of Railways and Canals had a survey or investigation made into the feasibility and cost of constructing a channel from the Devil's Elbow on the Holland river to a point in the neighbourhood of the Bradford Railway station, in South Simcoe?
2.	If not, wjll the department have this done at an early date, and if done, is the report favourable, and what is the estimated
cost?
The answer is:
1.	Yes.
2.	The Bradford survey was begun on the west branch of the Holland river at the junction of the Newmarket canal, which

point is 4-9 miles from the mouth of the river, Cook's bay, and carried up the west branch of the river to a point about 3 miles above the Bradford and Holland Landing road.
The canal or channel leading to the proposed basin in front of the Grand Trunk station, Bradford, would leave the west branch at the Devil's Elbow, 7 miles from Cook's bay, and the Bradford basin would be at 8-2 miles, or in otheV words the canal would be 1 -2 miles long with a bottom width of 50 feet. The proposed Bradford basin is estimated for 200 feet width, inclosed with concrete dock walls. No work is required in the 2 1 miles of river between the junction of the Newmarket canal and the Devil's Elbow. The estimated cost of the work is $52,947.

I wish to cal] the attention of the First Minister and of the government to a matter qf considerable importance, and one which we discussed last session. It is a question which is causing considerable feeling in southwestern Manitoba. I read from this morning's Ottawa 'Citizen'.
Stopped Pastor returning to Ireland from "Winnipeg via U.S.A.
1	(Special to the ' Citizen.')
Winnipeg, Dec. 6.-Rev. T. Davidson, famous pastor of Belfast, Ireland, who has been preaching special services here for several weeks left on Friday last for home via the United States. He was stopped at the boundary by immigration agents and compelled to return to Winnipeg to have papers filled out showing he was not an undesirable.
Such occurences are becoming so frequent that it is creating a strong feeling here. No one regrets it more than United States Consul General Jones, who is doing everything possible to create good feeling. He ascribes it all to ignorant and over zealous officials.
I did not suppose that I would be in order in discussing the question at this stage but it is certainly one which needs the serious consideration of the government. I refer to the manner in which the United States officials are dealing with people of almost all classes who are crossing over the boundary into the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We have no jurisdiction over the immigration officials of the United States. They exercise jurisdiction on their side of the line and we exercise jurisdiction on our side. I cannot give any answer to my hon. friend on this matter at all.

It seems to me that the Minister of the Interior and the government cannot afford to treat such a matter in this fashion. The Prime Minister will remember that last year we had a discussion over some rather outrageous cases and I think the Prime Minister himself promised that the matter would he looked into. Perhaps he can tell us if anything has been done, and if so what? Such things as these referred to by the hon. member (Mr. Schaffner) are indignities and we have no spirit unless we resent them. We ought at least try to make fair inquiry and see whether the conditions cannot be ameliorated.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I did not trust my memory about what occurred last session and I thought the Minister of the Interior would know. My impression is that representations have been made on this subject, but I will look into the matter and give further information to my hon. friend. I thought we had some arrangement about it.
Bill (No. 60) respecting the House of Commons.-Mr. Campbell.
GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals) moved second reading of Bill (No. 17) to authorize the government of Canada to acquire by lease lines of railways connected with the government railways.	j
Explain.

I explained this Bill on its introduction, and as the question of acquiring branch lines has been so thoroughly discussed in this House time and again, I think it hardly necessary to go into details. The Bill provides that the government shall have power to lease such line or lines as connect with the government railways and on the report of the board of management that such lines will be of benefit to the government railways. The Bill also provides that no line 'shall be taken over unless the chief engineer of the Department of Railways and Canals reports that it is in good order and in safe condition for operating. That provision is to obviate the necessity for expending a large amount of money on the line after it has been taken over. If it should be thought desirable to take over any line of railway under this Act, the government will not take it over unless the owners put it in such condition that we can operate it without having to undertake an expenditure on capital account to put that line into proper condition. In other words, we do not propose to lease any lines that are not workable and not in good operating order. The third clause is a safeguard to parliament that no line shall be leased and no contract of lease entered into without first submitting it to parliament for approval.
Is the tendency of this proposal along the lines of increasing government ownership? Is the government fully committed to that principle now and do they intend to work it out to its full extent?

That question covers a very vast territory, and I could hardly be expected to give an answer to it. If advantage be taken of this Act to lease any line or lines that now connect with the railway, on the face of it it certainly widens the field of government ownership.
And therefore it shows that the stories as to the government giving up the control and administration of the Intercolonial, are pure'fiction?

I do not clearly understand the necessity for this Bill. The minister has not stated what lines he has at present in view that might be taken over, but I assume it is his intention to follow out the proposal made by the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Emmerson) who has advocated from year to year the acquisition of these different lines by the government. I do not clearly understand the necessity of it. Why do you want authority from parliament to make a lease of these lines and afterwards come to parliament to ratify it? Why cannot you make a lease without the authority of parliament at all, and then come to parliament to get the lease ratified? I think that would have been the best plan. An acquisition of a property would be more fully considered if the whole of the reasons were to be given by the minister for the acquisition of a particular line. The pros and cons might be fully discussed, instead of the government coming to parliament with a cut and dried lease entered into by the government with the approval of the commission. That, I think, would be the more parliamentary course, and the better course to pursue if the government had not authority to enter into a lease, because once having entered into a lease, we -would have no power of altering or amending it; the lease would come to us holus bolus, take it or leave it. According to the other plan, if the lease was entered into conditionally without the government being bound until parliament had given its approval, I think that would be a far better plan than the one proposed by the Minister of Eailways. But the Minister of Eailways surely has some object in view, he has surely considered the question whether there are any railways in the maritime provinces which would, if acquired by the government, benefit the operation of the Intercolonial. If that be his object, he should take the House into his confidence and state what line he has in view, what railways he thinks would be for the benefit of the Intercolonial if they were acquired by the government.

My hon. friend is in error in thinking that I have some particular line or lines in view. The introduction of this Bill is the result of consideration by the government after repeated discussions in this House, and after considering, not only a report made by commissioners appointed by the New Brunswick government, but a report made by a commission appointed by this government over a year ago. They reported on some twenty railways in the provinces of Quebec, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. I am free to admit that I have not entered into the merits 'of any of these lines to ascertain which one or ones it would be Mr. W. F. MACLEAN.
proper for us to acquire. Until this year we have not had the machinery for that purpose which we have now, a body thoroughly well qualified, as I think the present board is, to judge of the merits of any of these lines, and to judge whether they might be of benefit and of how much benefit to the government line. That is the point of view from which the question would be approached. The other point of view, of course, would be the benefit of transportation to the people. But the first object, from my standpoint, would be the benefit that the leasing of these lines would be to the government system itself. As I say, I have not gone into the merits of any of these roads to see which ones if any we should lease. My hon. friend will see that any lease we might make, or any negotiations we might enter upon for making a lease, would always be made on the distinct understanding that they would not be binding until parliament gave its approval.
Would that mean that the government railway would not operate the lines until parliament approved?
Certainly.
I can hardly see the purpose of the Bill.

My hon. friend will understand that the government could have gone ahead without a Bill. We could have entered into negotiations without parliament having first said: We are agreeable, and if you find a line that will be of benefit to the government road, you may enter upon negotiations. By the passage of this Bill parliament approves of the principle of leasing any line or lines if they are found to be of benefit to the government system, although the details of such lease must be approved by parliament before they can become effective. One of the safeguards we will have in considering questions of that kind is the fact that the government line will not consider any proposition unless the board of management first approves or recommends it; and secondly, the chief engineer of the department must approve the standard of the road before the government will enter into negotiations for its acquisition, it being understood that an arrangement would not come into force until parliament had given its approval.

I would expect that the government would not propose a Bill like this unless they were prepared to inform the House whether it is the fixed policy of the government to extend the principle of government ownership of railways. If that is not their policy, it does not seem to be the part of wisdom to proceed along this line without some definite object in

view. I would naturally expect that the Minister of Railways had gone into an inquiry, through this board or through his chief engineer, with regard to the situation of the Intercolonial railway and the conditions which make it a non-paying concern, and that the object of these leases was to make it a paying concern in the future.
I think also he ought to be able to tell the House whether it is the determination of the government to go on and extend government ownership, because there is a great deal of controversy going on over that matter, some being in favour of it and some against it. I think there is a motion on the Order Paner for passing the Intercolonial over to some other railway to run it. Now, that indicates that there are some persons, at least from the maritime provinces, who are opposed to this principle. I think the Minister of Railways ought to he able to furnish such data to the House as will justify us in saying now that we are giving you a free hand, you have something in view, you have looked carefully over the ground, there are many feeders to this railway that would be valuable if put in good condition, providing we can lease them at a reasonable figure. But I agree with the ex-Minister of Railways (Hon. Mr. Haggart) that the government have such power already. Did they not do it with the Gibson railway, and with the Drummond County railway? Have they not done it several times during the last 14 or 15 years with reference to railways in the maritime provinces? Now, what different relation will the government be in with regard to this work after the Bill has been passed from what thev were in before? They could already make a lease subject to ratification bv parliament if they thought proper to do so. They will be able to do the same thing in future, so I cannot see what great benefit is going to be accomplished by this Bill. At any rate, if we pass the Bill it is assenting to the principle, and if that principle means the extension of government ownership of railways we ought to be given some better information than we possess at present. I am not opposing the Bill, but I think the Minister of Railways ought to be able to furnish the House with better data than he has, and a more elaborate scheme, and show us that he has carefully considered this subject, and that he thinks it will be wise for us to extend the principle.

I would be glad to give my hon. friend an outline of an elaborate scheme if I had one; but I frankly stated to the House what my view is, that it is proposed to obtain from parliament authority to have the Board of Management investigate any line that they think would be
beneficial to the government line of railways, and authority to lease any such line. As to the enlargement of government ownership, I am not prepared to announce any particular policy. The present policy of the government is public ownership of the Intercolonial railway; and so long as we own that line, which will probably be quite a while, I propose to make the best of it. But my hon. friend says there is a question on the Order Paper suggesting that the Intercolonial be leased. If the government were proposing to lease the _ government road, such a movement as this would neither help nor hinder the leasing of the government road. My own opinion is that if a company owned the Intercolonial, it would have had possession of some at least of these branch lines long before this. If it be true, .as has been argued time and again in this House, that the leasing of certain lines would not only improve the transportation facilities for the people, but also increase the usefulness of the government line, then parliament ought to be prepared to give us the power asked for in this Bill-to investigate and see if this -be true in any case, and, if so, to act accordingly.
Does the minister say that the government has not already the power to investigate a railway and enter into negotiations to lease without the passing of this Bill?

As I explained a few moments ago, the government can investigate this or any other question. But there is this difference, that with this measure on the statute book, parliament has approved of the principle of leasing any branch line which it may be found, after investigation, to be in the interest of the government railway to lease. We are starting on that investigation with the approval of parliament to the policy of leasing these lines if proper conditions do exist, the details to be submitted to parliament.

But the lease is not to become effective, I understood the minister to say, until it is submitted to parliament and is approved by parliament. If so, I cannot see the purpose of this Bill at all, unless as a meaningless sop offered to the member for Westmorland (Mr. Emmerson).

The Minister of Railways has perhaps properly described the effect of this Bill when he says that it gives the government a general authority to negotiate. He says, as I understand him, that general authority to negotiate ought to be granted by parliament, but in that case he should make it clear to us that there are some lines of railway in Quebec and in the maritime provinces which may usefully be acquired by * the Intercolonial railway, having regard to

the interests of the people in respect to transportation, and having regard to the interests of the Intercolonial railway as a going concern. I may say in passing that I rather object to the expression of government ownership. I would like the government to understand that they do not own the Intercolonial railway. They are for the time being, unfortunately for the people of this country, entrusted with its management and control; but the railway is owned by the people of Canada, and not by the government at all. I must confess that 1 would have expected the Minister of Railways and Canals, according to his own definition, to have given us a little more information than he has given us so far. He has not made it clear that, in his own opinion, there are any railways of that character. He has referred us to certain reports of certain gentlemen appointed by this government and certain other gentlemen appointed by the government of New Brunswick, who have arrived at certain conclusions. I am not very familiar with these reports, and the minister appears to be no more familiar. However, he has not stated to what extent he has acepted their conclusions, nor has he given us the name of any railway which he thinks it advisable for the government to acquire. More than that, he has not intimated to us the principle upon which the government or the Government Railway Management Board will proceed in dealing with this question. Although the minister very cleverly introduced into his speech words that are not in the Bill, I do not observe in the Bill itself any statement of policy upon which the Government Railway Management Board will proceed. I understand that they have full discretionary powers of management and control so far as the operation of the Intercolonial railway is concerned; but I do not understand what discretionary powers they are to have in regard to leasing branch lines. I do not understand what considerations they are to have regard to in coming to a conclusion. The Bill leaves us entirely ignorant on this point, and the minister also leaves us ignorant of that. If the minister asks us for this Bill as a general authority to negotiate, and that is all it can amount to, ought he not to give to the House some explanation of the principles upon which they will proceed to negotiate-what considerations they will have regard to and upon what lines they will proceed, in coming to a conclusion as to whether they shall recommend or not? I can understand that the Intercolonial railway might embark upon a policy of acquiring ultimately every one of these branch lines. That is perfectly intelligible whether we approve of it or not. I can understand that the policy might be very much more restricted than that-that it might relate only to such of these lines as would in the immediate fu-Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
ture become financially profitable to the Intercolonial railway as a going concern. I can understand that lines would be acquired because they would give increased transportation facilities to the people, and although not immediately profitable, would become profitable within a reasonable period. There are other lines of policy that might be suggested. The minister does not commit himself to anything, and only asks for general power to negotiate. He does not give us the slightest idea of the lines on which the action of the government or the Railway Management Board is to be conducted. I am bound to say that I am in favour, so far as I am personally concerned, of coming to parliament first and stating what the government proposes to do and getting this general authority to negotiate. I think that, perhaps, on the whole-although there may be a difference of opinion-that is the wiser and fairer course to pursue. But I do not think it a very advantageous course to pursue unless we get from the minister some intimation of the lines upon which the general power to negotiate will be exercised and the policy which will influence the government in coming to a conclusion, one way or the other, with regard to any of these lines.

I would like very much to have a little more light on this question. When it comes to a vote, I propose to vote on this Bill. At the present juncture, I do not know whether I shall vote for it or against it. Unless I get a little more light on the subject, a little more information than I have now, I shall be strongly inclined to vote against it. I think that the minister must surely have had in mind, when he prepared that Bill, some branch railways or some number of branch railways that he was going to acquire. For myself,
I would like to have some definite information what branches are to be taken in. Is it for a few branches in New Brunswick that are not paying a dividend and never will pay a dividend, under present management? Is it for some branches in the province of Quebec that are in trouble? Is it for certain branches in Nova Scotia that are not paying dividends? I remember that, last autumn, a commission was appointed to examine and report on the subject of branch railways. And I was astonished to learn afterwards that the most prosperous branch, the branch that runs through the best part of the maritime provinces, the Dominion Atlantic railway, had not been examined or reported on at all. This road, as many hon. members know, runs through the richest part of the maritime provinces
Oh, oh.

Perhaps the hon. member for Pictou ','Ir. Macdonald) does not know,

but I know that this road runs through the richest part of the maritime provinces; that we send over that road between half a million and a million barrels of apples alone every year; that the country through which it runs is handicapped by that railway, a country that would be alive with manufactures if we had a railway that was assisting manufacturing development, in stead of taking out of the manufacturers all they can. This is a railway which is managed from London, and anything in Canada managed from London has hardly ever been prosperous so far as Canadians are concerned. I say I was astounded to learn that this road had never been examined or reported on by the commissioners. And when I inquired the reason, I found that there had been a difference between the management of that road and the commission in regard to the cost of running over the road. I believe-of course, I am not speaking positively, but the information came to me from a very good source-the management wanted $30 a day for taking the commissioners over the road, and the commissioners, in an economical frame of mind, refused to give it, and made no report on the road. I should like to know, before I vote, if it is contemplated to take over the Dominion Atlantic as one of the branches of the Intercolonial. It can be bought, and it is not in bankruptcy. All that any one has to do is to look at the report sent to the government every year, and he will find it to be a good paying road. A part of it is leased from the Intercolonial railway. This private company actually leases part of its road from the Intercolonial. And it is one of the best paying pieces of road in Canada. I would like to know if the government intend to withdraw that lease. It was a foolish lease in the beginning, it has been a foolish lease so far as as the people of Nova Scotia are concerned ever since, and it will continue to be a foolish lease until the end. I repeat that I should like very much to have a little more information before deciding whether I shall oppose this Bill or support it.
How would it do to use this power as a means to extend the Intercolonial westward to Georgian bay?

I have opposed any further purchase, lease or administration of any railway in addition to what the government possesses. And I oppose it now. And I am prepared to say that, unless things happen that should change my mind-and they will have to be very real and important things, I shall oppose it for many years to come.

The Bill before us is, to my mind, an extraordinary one; it is
something new, I think, in the way of railway legislation. The powers asked for by the government are very unusual, and they are asked upon a basis of very little information as to how the Bill will actually be carried into effect. I understand that the Bill will authorize the government to lease certain railways-we do not know what railways, nor do we know whether they are rich corporations or poor ones. They may be corporations whose bonds are not worth ten cents on the dollar; but the moment the government gets this power to lease these roads, no doubt the bonds will go up very quickly. To my mind, there is an open door there for a good speculation on the part of some one down in New Brunswick or Quebec. I should like more information before we are called upon to vote on the question. I do not wish to oppose anything that is in the interests of the Intercolonial railway or will promote the interests of the maritime provinces or Quebec in relation to their railway systems. But it does seem to me that there is something about this Bill that is rather dark. Under it, the Minister of Railways is to be authorized to lease certain roads in whole or in part, in fact, any line or lines connected with the government railway. And he is authorized to do this upon the recommendation of the Government Railways Managing Board. In effect, the Minister of Railways is authorized to do this on his own recommendation, because, practically, the Minister of Railways and the Managing Board of the Intercolonial are one and the same power-I do not think they are very far apart yet. I confess that the legislation is of a character new to me; it seems to me to give the Minister of Railways extraordinary powers. Now, if the recommendations of the government Railways Managing Board would go so far as to tell before the purchase is gone into who the owners of the railway are, and what is the value of the road, whether it is a bankrupt road or one paying dividends, and so on, I could see my way more clearly to giving the minister this power. But, if the Bill passes, he is to get this power without our having any information as to the value of the road or roads to be leased. That, to my mind, is a very strong objection, and I think the minister ought to see his way to remedying that defect. I assume that the minister will not press this to a conclusion at once, but that he will give members a further opportunity of looking into the matter and by all means that he will be able to place before the House, before the Bill passes its second reading, definite information with regard to the names of the railways he proposes to purchase, their value, the value of their securities and the holders of these securities, practically a statement of the persons who are to be benefited by this leasing or

purchase. It looks to me like a dark horse. I think we are taking a great deal for granted if we confer on the minister a power like this on the limited information he has given.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am afraid the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) is unduly suspicious. It never occurred to me that there was anything very dark or dangerous about the Bill; it seemed one of the most moderate and reasonable Bills ever submitted to parliament and I should be surprised if, after a fair consideration of the Bill, there is any serious opposition to it. The adoption of this Bill simply asserts a principle which has frequently found expression in the debates of this House and which every . man in any way acquainted with railway matters will readily approve. That principle is that where there are branch lines connected with a large and important system it would undoubtedly be in the interest of economy and efficiency that these branch lines should be consolidated with the general system if such a consolidation can be brought about on fair and reasonable terms. It needs no argument to say that a short branch line of railway may be economically a failure, its expensive management may be so great that it cannot pay even its working expenses. Take that same branch line and consolidate it with a large system and instead of a burden it might become a useful feeder to the larger system. Any hon. gentleman who has the slightest knowledge of railways will at once agree to this general principle. It is well known that along the line of the Intercolonial railway there are a number of branches worked more or less inefficiently-I will not say more or less efficiently, some of them are not worked efficiently, and it is believed that if these branches were consolidated with the Intercolonial railway better results could be obtained. I do not agree with the hon. gentlemen opposite that it is essential to specify what branches are in contemplation. For myself I have no idea of a single branch which will be leased under this Bill, while I have no doubt that some branches will be acquired by way of lease. The criticism of the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Haggart) rather goes to the fact that the minister will have to come back to parliament for approval. That goes to show that the Minister of Railways has not been taking to himself some unwarranted power but has been unduly modest. He does not ask authority to enter into any binding arrangement with anybody but he does ask the House to accept the principle involved in this Bill that the consolidation of branch lines with the Intercolonial railway is a desirable thing if it can be brought about on fair and reasonable terms. Any branch of the Intercolonial railway may properly be brought within the operation of this Bill.
Mr. HENDERSON

My criticism was confined to the absence of any statement by the minister as to the principle upon which the government intended to proceed. What will be the government's policy after getting this power to negotiate? I approve of their coming here to get the power to negotiate as I have said, but I think we are entitled to some statement of what the policy of the government will be.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is certainly desirable that there should be as clear an understanding as possible, but my hon. friend will agree that inasmuch as we must come back to parliament for approval, even although the government should be unwise enough not to negotiate in the right direction, the rights of parliament are fully protected. The Bill sets forth, in the first place, that the road must be in good and safe condition. There is a very important assertion of principle. If you take a dilapidated road and acquire it by lease, although on the surface it may seem to be a good arrangement, you may have to spend a large amount in putting it in order. Therefore the Minister of Railways has wisely determined that he will not consider the acquisition of any branch line unless it is in a safe condition.
Railway managers often take over a road just because it is in a poor condition and put it in good order.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No doubt there might be cases where the Minister of Railways would say to the parties: Your road is not in a condition to enable me to negotiate for it; put it in a substantial position so that we will not have to spend a large amount of money on it and we will deal with you. There are a number of railways that might be acquired, notably in New Brunswick. There are very few in Nova Scotia that wouid be willing to be called branch lines. The hon. member for Hants (Mr. Black) has spoken of the Dominion Atlantic. I am afraid the Dominion Atlantic would be offended if it were called a branch line.
I do not mind offending them, they have offended us often enough.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: People are often very glad to get railway accommodation and when they get it are sometimes too ready to find fault with the railway company. However that may be, I think the House ought to adopt the principle of this Bill. It is a principle of what might be called the economy of railway management.
The Dominion Atlantic could come under this.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
It is not confined to branch lines, it is any line connecting. It might be a railway 1,000 miles in length.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It might be, but we have not any railways of that length down there.
It might be anywhere, it might be the Canadian Northern.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think there is any danger of a branch of 1,000 miles in length being brought under this Bill and anyhow, as we must come back to parliament for ratification of any agreement made, my hon. friend will see that the public interests are adequately protected. This Bill simply authorizes the Minister of Railways to enter upon the consideration of a policy that has again and again found advocates on both sides of this House. True the minister could have gone ahead made his negotiations and then come back to parliament, but he has thought it best to pursue the policy, which I am glad to say has won the approval of the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden), of coming here and asking a general declaration in favour of the principle. I would take it for granted that the managing board would have to satisfy the Minister of Railways that the road will either from the beginning or at a very early stage pay its own working expenses and a sufficient sum to protect the government against loss. That leads me to repeat the observation I ventured to make that it is quite possible a branch railway which is losing money as a branch line might even make a little when consolidated with the general system. I think the Bill is reasonable, I think the criticism of the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. John Haggart) that we do not need to come to parliament as we have the power to negotiate without coming to parliament, while true is not important; in fact I think it is much wiser that the minister should come here and ask parliament to give general approval to the principle laid down and then I think it is not too much to ask the House to believe that the Minister of Railways and the managing board will not recommend the acquisition, even by way of lease, of any railway which would not be a helper to the Intercolonial railway. But if the Minister of Railways should be so unwise as to do that and if his colleagues in the government should be so unwise as to encourage him to do it, you still have the safeguard of this House of Commons and this parliament, because no lease that the minister might propose could be of any binding effect until it had been submitted to this House and had received the approval of parliament.

The hon. member for Hants (Mr. Black) was asking for light a little while ago. I watched him quite closely while the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) was diffusing such light as he has diffused on this Bill; I did not see much of
an answering gleam on the face of my hon. friend, and when the Minister of Finance got up I noticed that my hon. friend fixed [DOT]both eyes on him. I do not believe I am far astray when I venture the guess that no very great light has gone into the cranium of the hon. member for Hants as a result of the explanation or the diffusing of light by the hon. Finance Minister.
I am still waiting for light.

Still waiting! Then, I want to give the hon. member for Hants some of the light he was asking for. If he will just remove the little blur before his eyes and look back and down he will see a certain figure, not long ago upon the ministerial benches. He will see that that figure is no longer on the ministerial benches, but is removed a little farther to the right, and he will remember that that gentleman has had for some years a veTy decided liking for the absorption of maritime province railways by the Intercolonial railway, that he has advocated it in the country before his constituents, advocated it in the House, that he has pestered and bothered the present Minister of Railways and Canals considerably by the persistent advocacy and criticism which accompanied that advocacy, and that as a result the Minister of Railways, bothered with the fellow, gave a commission and had some of his wise men sail around about the maritime provinces. They had a good time, looked over all these roads, drew their money, got their expenses and then prepared a report for him which, strange to say, the Minister of Railways has not yet read. Am I wrong in that?
My hon. friend is wrong to this extent, that it was laid on the table last year and he should have read it if he has not.
I am not talking about myself. The hon. member for Hants has not been asking me for light.
But you are attempting to give it to him.
And I thought that it was a fair assumption from what the minister said that he had not looked within the pages of the report. Has he?
I have read it through twice.

Then, if my hon. friend has read it through twice, it is a very poor report or he would be able to give his opinions in reference to it. Now, he certainly says that he has not 'bestowed any thought upon it at all. Meanwhile the hon. member for Westmorland, still somewhat critical, a little on the offside, bothers the minister again, and the minister says: I

will have another whack at him; I will put some enabling measure on the law-book; I will have a statute that will enable me to take in these railways. Of course, I am not going to bestow any bother upon looking into the question whether there are or are not any roads. This is sufficient for my purpose at the present time. My purpose is to get another stepping stone away from that bothersome man from Westmorland. That is about all the light there is in it except that a little more may be shed upon it in this way. I see a splendid arrangement for future good work about the time of the coming elections. The minister comes down and says: Here is a matter of sufficient gravity to be called to the attention of two hundred and odd gentlemen whose time is precious and who are here to consider serious, honest and earnest legislation. He first calls the attention of his colleagues to it and says: This is the measure that I propose to bring down, and then he calls the attention of the House to it. When he calls the attention of the House to it, asks them to pass it, and they ask him for his policy he has no more policy than the man in the moon. He cannot teil us whether he believes there are any roads that would come under this category. He does not say whether he will find the branches in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick or Quebec, or whether he will use this power as a possible negotiating instrument to obtain a road and join it on to the Intercolonial railway at the city of Montreal running to the Great I ,akes, or a road running across the prairies, or a road running all the way across to the Pacific ocean, because, under the enabling power of this Act, he can enter into negotiations with the Canadian Pacific railway to-morrow or any day and can acquire these roads by lease, provided they axe willing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But he could do that without the Act.

He could do that without the Act, but let me tell you what I say is the difference between doing it with and without the Act. You have done it without an Act. The government have done things equal to this and like it, as the government are doing time after time. Instance after instance is given. But, there is this difference which is two-fold. The moment you pass this Act everybody knows that the minister will have every branch and small railway which joins with or is in close proximity to the Intercolonial railway on his back and he will no longer have the advantage of being able to say to them:	The government has not made
up its mind in reference to this; I have no authority for this sort of thing. The best I can do would be to make a sort of arrangement with you and to take it to parliament. But the moment the Act is Mr. FOSTER.
passed he is in a very different position, they come to him and say:	You have no
excuse for not entering into negotiations for this road. Here is a branch road, we want you to take it over; what is your excuse for not doing it? You have the approval of the House to do the very thing that we are asking you to do. Does not the minister see that his powers of resistance are absolutely taken away from him and he cannot help but enter into negotiations with them and yield to their pressure? Then, when it comes down to the House, the House itself is restricted and restrained when the minister rises and says:	Here
is the report of my board of managers, here is the report of my engineer, I am doing exactly what parliament has sanctioned and ordered to be done under certain conditions and why are you opposing it? So, the power is made all the greater as against any opposing force because the government would say: We have the authority of parliament; we have simply entered into a contract with the authority of parliament and it must be passed. It is difficult for the opposition, even though part of it is composed of men on the government side, to make headway against a government measure when it is brought down for the first time, but it is infinitely more difficult when it is brought down in sequence of a measure that approves of the principle involved in the transaction. The House will have committed itself to the principle once it passes this Act, and that is the reason why I rather agree with my hon. friend the late Minister of Railways and Canals in reference to this matter. But there has not been a single assertion made by the government or the minister who is bringing down this measure as to how extensive or how limited this power may be. Does the minister think this proper to ask us to confirm a power which might be applied to all the great railways of the country because they all merge into either the city of Montreal, or the city of Quebec, as well as the points along the Intercolonial railway. It is of continental application and the ministers, in bringing in their Bill, do not even say that they do not contemplate going beyond branch lines. It is giving them a tremendous omnibus power and this parliament is binding itself that if certain conditions are fulfilled they may carry out the operation. Then, there is another point in connection with the matter and it was hinted at by my hon. friend from Halton. What a splendid avenue this opens up to the ingenious and skilful schemer. Here is an omnibus proposition. Here are some people who to-day own the bonds of a crippled railway. They say: The government has the power to take this railway over and operate it. Once it is taken over and operated and the blood of the Intercolonial railway system runs in its deadened veins,

it will suddenly come to the point of not only sustaining itself but of giving profits, and what a splendid avenue it opens up to companies of every kind to bring influence upon the minister and the government to negotiate with reference to the absorption of a certain road and possibly to carry it out. We will wake up after the negotiations have carried through probably to the fact that somebody has got the worthless bonds, worthless up to that time and that these people will then have made a fortunate speculation for themselves. As to the recommendation upon which the minister acts, what does it amount to as it is outlined in this section? Nothing at all. They need not give a single reason to the minister. If the minister communes with himself or with his creatures for he is the creator of these creatures; if he communes with himself and satisfies himself he takes that part of himself which is outside himself, to wit his board of managers and he says; Write me a recommendation. They write him a recommendation which may be in five lines or less and he comes down to the House with that recommendation and it is not worth a hill of beans simply because it is not a reasoned recommendation. He does not provide for a reasoned recommendation in this Bill and he ought to provide for it. The grounds upon which the recommendation is based should be set out and should become the property of the House when they are asked to consider the matter. It does seem to me that the minister and the government have not thought about this thing sufficiently to give us light on it. I join in the pitiful cry of the member for Hants:	Light, more light upon this
subject before we can consider it.

This little preliminary discussion has swung in a rather wide circle ranging from the position of my hon. friend from York that this Bill had absolutely no meaning whatever, to the wild flights of imagination indulged in by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Foster). Now that we have had these preliminary fireworks it might be well for us to consider just what this proposition really means. We do not need to soar to imagination nor descend to misrepresentation to arrive at the proper conclusion which is quite apparent to any one who looks at the measure with calmness and deliberation. It is nothing more nor less than that the government has asked this House to affirm the principle that it would be desirable for them to go into the question of obtaining a lease of certain branch lines along the Intercolonial railway to be utilized as feeders thereof and in connection therewith. My hon. friend from Toronto has no doubt overlooked the preamble of this measure which expressly limits the railways to be leased under this Act to such railways as are feeders of and are in connection with the Intercolonial railway. I do think that this proposition is sufficiently important to engage the attention of hon. members in a somewhat more serious discussion. Is it wise that this parliament should say to the government that they should look into the question of what branch lines lying along the Intercolonial railway would be advantageous to the people of the country generally as well as to the people of the country living along the lines of the railways in question. We have had the matter discussed at various sessions in the abstract, but parliament has never declared one way or the other on the proposition, and now this Bill asks for a declaration in favour of it. Of course hon. gentlemen know that it is impossible for the minister to say that he proposes to lease this, that or the other railway, but it is well within the knowledge of every member of this House that last year a return was brought down showing that after investigation it was found that there were 15 branch railways lying along the Intercolonial. Some of which it might be advisable to incorporate with that trunk line of railway. Let me premise by saying that so far as the operation of the Intercolonial is concerned, after you leave the city of Quebec and until you come to Campbellton it can hardly be said that the Intercolonial strikes any point that is accessible to the ocean. From Campbellton you run through a country that does not connect with any ocean port until you come to St. John; thence you run along to Halifax and the railway touches at one or two points only in Nova Scotia which are available for ocean transportation.
Could you not connect at Metapedia and get an ocean port along the Bay Chaleur to Gaspe?
That railway is only constructed to Paspebiac.
That is an ocean port.

The railway is not yet constructed to Gaspe, and we have the Intercolonial railway in the anomalous position that with the exception of some points in Nova Scotia and at St. John, the whole of that vast range of coast along the maritime provinces is not reached directly by the Intercolonial but is reached by some 15 or 16 branch lines. That is a condition of affairs that invites attention. Some of us dream of the time when this country will be sufficiently self-contained that at least in the winter season we will be able to control Canadian exports through Canadian ports, and make our own ports the avenue through which will come our imports. That seems to me to be a laudable idea and one which we should aim to attain. And, in order that we may control the traffic to the sea the proposition now before us be-

comes a very important one. What this Bill does is that it asks parliament to say whether or not parliament approves of the idea of incorporating these branch line feeders with the trunk line. Upon the wisdom of that proposition a gentleman of such wide experience as Mr. Tiffin, the traffic manager of the Intercolonial, and formerly of the Canadian Pacific railway, and Mr. Story, say:
The want of proper facilities for the conduct of even the existing traffic is detrimentally affecting the business interests of the districts interested in these branches, and preventing that development of industries, enhancement of property values, and general betterment that would undoubtedly follow on an improved service.
The present branches are hampered by lack of capital and insufficient equipment, and are not in a financial position to increase their inadequate traffic facilities, and the absorption of these lines into the Intercolonial system would beyond question result in a greatly improved condition of affairs.	_
It is a well established fact that in nearly every case where branch lines have been absorbed by trunk lines, and extended markets have thus been opened up for business along the main lines, such a policy has not only proved to be of great value to the branch lines, but lias provided additional revenue for the main line, they becoming valuable feeders, increasing the traffic and the earning powers of the trunk lines.
One need not argue that proposition further. The magnificent success which has attended the Canadian Pacific railway throughout this country and which has made it the pride of every Canadian, has been very largely due to the wise policy of its directors in reaching out here and there and absorbing the feeders of the Canadian Pacific railway which has developed the territory through which they ran. The position of the Minister of Railways simply is: that the government should be permitted to look into the advisability of acquiring the branch lines and feeders of the peoples' railway as the Canadian Pacific railway and the Grand Trunk and other railway systems in Canada have done with regard to their connecting lines. To that proposition the House cannot fail to give assent. The interests concerned are not merely local or provincial but they are great national issues in that the object sought is to obtain an outlet for the Intercolonial Tailway to the various ocean ports of the maritime provinces and a connection with the mineral resources of these provinces. As to whether or not any one is to be injured by the minister entering into negotiations for the purpose of obtaining a lease of a railway which is in proper condition for operation, I think the Bill throws around that the very proper safeguard that nothing can be eventually done without the sanction of parliament.
I venture to say that my hon. friend from North Toronto, who conjured up some difficulties that might result from the adoption of this Bill, would not be deterred from the most energetic opposition to any proposal which the Minister of Railways might bring down if he chose to think that the proper thing to do was to oppose it. It is perfectly understood thak, the House does not commit itself to the adoption of any particular proposal under this Act until it is submitted; but by this Bill, if it is adopted, parliament will commit itself to the proposal that it is wise that the Intecolonial railway should enter upon the policy of incorporating branch lines.
Will the hon. member tell me what difference there is between the power the Minister of Railways and the government possess now and the power they will possess after this Bill passes?

If my hon. friend had listened to the argument of his hon. leader who sits beside him, he would not have found it necessary to ask me that question. The hon. leader of the opposition and the hon. member for North Toronto both made it clear that this Bill does do a veTy important and serious thing, in that it declares that the policy of this country shall be to incorporate with the Intercolonial railway such branch lines as it may be advantageous to the country to incorporate with it, and the minister is authorized to go on and negotiate subject to the ratification of this House. It affirms an important principle that has never before been affirmed by parliament, and for that reason this is an important measure. The question of the acquisition of branch lines is one in which not only the people of the maritime provinces, but the people of the whole of Canada, are interested. 1 would like as a sequence to this proposition that my hon. friend the Minister of Railways would look into one or two other matters relating to the extension of the Intercolonial railway. The construction of a line of railway from Moncton to Pugwash, along the north shore of Nova Scotia, and the construction of a comparatively small addition from New Glasgow to Country Harbour in Guysboro would give the people of this country a line of railway exactly the same in length as that part of the Intercolonial now running from Moncton to Halifax, and would place the oceangoing trade 100 miles nearer to the other side it is at present by the line to Halifax.
And by a good port too.
That is a matter beyond doubt. I have frequently pressed this proposal on the minister privately. It is to be hoped that

the people of Canada generally will appreciate the ambition of this little province down by the sea, that as we go on developing Canada it may more and more become the entry and the exit for the trade of this country. We look to measures such as the one before the House as hastening the time when our ideas and ambitions in that respect may be realized.

I would like to ask the hon. gentleman if he can point to any Act on the statutes of this country that enacts a theory. I have always thought that parliament enacted something, and not merely a theory or a principle without anything being done.
My hon. friend will find that this proposal is no mere theory, but a very practical piece of legislation which I hope will be for the good of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. E. M. Macdonald) appears to think that the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Geo. E. Foster) has been indulging in a little imagination. On the contrary, I think that what the hon. member for North Toronto said is very hard business, and it is just the kind of business that I would expect from him. Before I heard a word that he uttered, I had prepared and intended to introduce an amendment on the very point he raised, and I do not think I am much given to imagination. The hon. member for Pictou tells us that everything is made right by the preamble-that satisfies the general idea. But the point is that the preamble does not say how much of the preamble is to be looked to by the minister, how much by the board of management and how much by the chief engineer. When we come to clause 3, however we find how very little the board of management have to do. The minister will go to his board of management and will say: Do you think we ought to lease such a railway or such half dozen railways? And they will say:	Perhaps we ought to, the line
would be more or less valuable to the government railway; yes, we recommend that. Then the minister enters into negotiation and ascertains what the terms are likely to be; but there is not a word in that clause that requires him to obtain from the board of management their approval of the terms. It is very little use to ask, as protection to the people of this country, the approval of the board of management unless that approval covers the terms of the lease, and that is the very question raised by the hon. member for North Toronto. Now, I propose to ask the House to amend that clause to that effect. Then we shall have a recommendation that will be worth something to us. I might very easily re-36
commend the minister to take a lease of a piece of property; but when I saw the terms of the lease. I might advise him not to have anything to do with it on those terms. I hope the minister will not object to making that point clear. So far as I am concerned, if it is made perfectly clear, I approve his getting the recommendation from his board of management, which consists of practical railway men and experts in railway management. In committee I propose to move an amendment to that effect.

I think the hon. gentleman is mistaken with respect to the purport of this section 3. The recommendation of the Government Railways Managing Board must cover the whole terms of the lease, and it is only the report of the chief engineer that relates to the good and safe condition of the road. So that objection appears to me to be removed by the terms of section 3 of the Bill itself. I think it is a matter of common knowledge to this House that the Intercolonial needs some extension in order that it may become efficient and effective, and serve the country through which it runs. It is also a matter of common knowledge to this House that there are many branch roads connecting with the Intercolonial which it would be in the interest of that system to acquire. It appears to me, therefore that there is some soundness in the contention that this Bill does not give any additional power to the Minister of Railways, but is merely an intimation that this parliament supports him in the endeavour he contemplates making to add to the effectiveness of the service of the Intercolonial. Ample protection is thrown around the whole operation under this section, by providing at the end that any lease made under it is of no effect until ratified by the parliament of Canada.

I do not think it is necessary to add much to what has been said. I assure the House that this Bill was nob introduced, as the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) thinks, to placate a certain gentleman lest by his continual coming he might weary me. It is a sincere desire to make the best possible out of the government railway; that is the only desire I have, not to try to serve any friends, or disconcert any enemies. I want to make it clear to the House that my Bill is introduced with the object in view of taking parliament into the entire confidence of the _ government, and having a decision on this question before we enter upon negotiations; and then, after negotiations have been entered upon, to submit the details to parliament for ratification. We want everything to be done openly and above board, after the fullest investigation and scrutiny are made. I can assure my



1124
hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker), who discussed this question from a practical point of view, that I certainly thought I had covered the point he has mentioned. The minister does not propose to enter upon negotiations to lease any line unless upon the recommendation of the board, which recommendation shall include the terms of the lease also. Certainly that is my intention, and if it is not clear we will make it clear in committee. I assure the House again that this Bill is for the sole purpose of rendering, if possible, the government railways more efficient. We take the step in the interest of the public and of the government line, and if it is found after investigation by practical men, that they are lines, the leasing of which would bring about this object, then we will proceed to negotiate for a lease.
Might I ask if any applications have been made to the government, or any negotiations have been entered into with any branch line company?
The only discussion I have had as to branch lines, hon. gentlemen have heard it all in the House. There has been no application for leasing any line from any company that has come to my knowledge.

Allow me briefly to draw the distinction between the position of the government before this Bill is passed and their position after it is passed. The House and the minister must remember that by the passage of this Bill we affirm the principle that branch lines may be a necessity of government railways, and we empower the government to enter into arrangements for acquiring them. When we affirm the principle and give power to the government, it is the duty of the government to acquire them. Look at the different position you are in after the passage of this Bill from the position you are in before. Before, the option was left entirely with the government to enter into an arrangement of this kind or not; but after the passage of this Bill, if my reasoning is correct, it is compulsory upon the government to do so, you have1 no longer an option. If a branch line, or any railway that connects with the Intercolonial, is considered to be necessary for the Intercolonial, and will increase the earnings of the Intercolonial, we affirm the principle that under certain circumstances the government must acquire that branch line. My contention is that you are not merely passing an empowering Act, but you are laying down a principle which the government must enforce. Now I differ from my hon. friend the leader of the opposition, who thought perhaps it was best to come to parliament and get the power. He qualified that statement, however, by saying that the principle should be laid down before Mr. GRAHAM.
exercising the power, and that a principle could be laid, down in an Act _ of_ parliament which would guide the commission in making the inquiry, and the government in exercising the option. The better plan I think the government may act upon at the present time. If they think, in the interests of this road, that it is desirable to enter into an agreement with branch line companies to acquire their property, then let the government come to parliament and get the necessary power, after they have obr tained the opinion of the board of management that the road is likely to be useful to the Intercolonial, and the opinion of the chief engineer that the road is in a proper condition. Then parliament would authorize the government to go on and acquire the road.

I am sorry to disagree with my hon. friend from Lanark (Mr. Hag-gart), who is much older and more experienced than myself in these matters. But.
I cannot see that if we adopt the principle of authorizing the Minister of Railways and his board of management to inquire whether it w'ould be well to acquire a branch line or lines, that we thereby force the government to do so. I do not believe there is anything in the whole Bill that would suggest such a thing. If the Bill is not clear enough on the question that the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) raised, let it be made clear, but I think it is perfectly clear. When I read the Bill I thought that was the intention of the Minister of Railways, but if that intention is not clear let it be made clear. Now as I am not of a suspicious turn of mind like my hon. friends of the opposition, who think that this Bill hides some sinister purpose, I must say that for my part I commend the Minister of Railways for coming to this House and asking us to lay down a principle before he proceeds with the investigation of any particular road with a view of taking it over. I understand it is the intention that the board shall investigate any particular road which in their judgment they think would be serviceable in increasing the earning power of the Intercolonial. If this board are not capable of doing that, they are not capable of managing the Intercolonial, they are not capable of doing what they are supposed to be doing now.
Therefore, as I think, personally, that thev are capable, and as I think the minister is wholly capable. I believe this House runs no risk in trusting to this board the further addition to their duties of examining into whether branch railways will be a benefit to this railway or not. The principle of branch railways has been adopted not only by the great roads of this country but by the great roads of the United States as well. Feeders are absolutely necessary in order to get re-

turns, and it is returns we want, after all, from the Intercolonial. I believe that when we have the statement of the Intercolonial before usi, it will show that we were justified in appointing this board of management. As I have stated before, that I believe we do not run any risk. The minister has to come back to this House with all the terms and particulars; he. has to get sanction for every piece of road he proposes to take over. It seems to me there is no reason for the suspicion which seems to exist in the minds of some hon. members, judging by the expressions we have heard this afternoon. We must trust to a very large extent to the management. The minister has to report to the governor in council and get their sanction and he has to get also the sanction of parliament. How can it be necessary to hedge him around more than with these precautions? Again I say that, for my part, I commend the minister for asking the authority of this House to the principle before taking action.

I quite agree with the hon. member for South Lanark (Mr. Hag-gart) that the passage of this Bill will mean the affirmation by this House of the principle of the acquirement of branch roads. Upon that ground alone I am prepared to support the measure now before the House. It was not my intention to speak on this subject, because it seemed to me obvious that the Bill ought to' pass. Privately-owned railways, whether in Canada or elsewhere, make their business successful in proportion as they acquire or build feeders for their lines, and, if the Intercolonial is to be run as a business proposition, to my mind It is obvious that it must acquire feeders along its route. So much from that standpoint; but there is another phase of the question which has not been discussed at all, and one to my mind that is of vital importance to the people of the constituency in which I live in common with many others in the maritime provinces and in' Quebec. That point is that where there is a multiplicity of small railwavs, a shipper of freight who lives on a branch line has to pay two, and sometimes three, freights. In my own county, for instance, to send freight' for a distance of only twelve miles in a certain direction three railways must be used. I sneak of freight shipped from River Hebert via Maecan to Springhill. The freight miyst be sent over the Maritime Coal, Railway and Power Company's line to Maccan, then over the Intercolonial to Springhill Junction, and then over the Cumberland Railway and Coal Company's line to Springhill. Consequently, to cover this distance of nineteen miles a shipper is called upon to pay a larger sum for freight 36}
than he would have to pay for perhaps 100 miles over a line of railway owned by a single company or by the government, as the case may be. Without discussing the question further, I wish to say that I am in hearty accord with the principle of the Bill, and if it comes to a vote it is my intention to vote for it.
I desire
The hon. member has spoken.
Others have spoken twice
I did not call attention to the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) speaking in answer to a question.
But. the hon. member for South Lanark (Mr. Haggart) spoke twice, and he is not a minister of the Crown.
Go on.
Have I the right, Mr. Speaker, to ask a question?

I would warn the House that if the right to speak twice is given to one member, it can hardly be refused to another. The. rule is against, but it is for the House to say whether the rule is to be lived up to.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Only a question.
I suppose a question might be allowed.

Before this vote is taken, I wish to ask the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) if the refusal of his commission to examine and report on the Dominion Atlantic railway means that the minister does not consider that the Dominion Atlantic is a branch or connection of the Intercolonial and so is barred from the operation of this Bill? I feel very strongly on this subject, because we have been for years paying two freights on almost everything imported into that country. If we get a barrel of flour from Montreal, we pay two freights; if we get a parcel by express, two express charges must be paid. All our manufacturers who export have to pay double freight, and so have all the people who import goods into that country. I cannot help feeling waTmly on this question, because the interests of the -people I represent, the prosperity of the manufacturers and importers are vitally concerned. So far as the Act of the commissioners is concerned, I think they treated the country from Windsor to Annapolis not exactly very courteously. I would like to know in what position the Dominion Atlantic railway stands in regard to this scheme before I cast my vote.

That is a pretty long question; I am afraid it will take a long answer. As to the latter part of what the hon. member (Mr. Black) says, it rather proves what has been said before, that the Intercolonial so far as rates are concerned, is more beneficial to a community than an ordinary company road, else my hon. friend would not prefer that the Intercolonial should have the Dominion Atlantic. The second part of the hon. member's question is easily answered: There is nothing that would preclude the Dominion Atlantic from coming within the scope of this Bill.
Mr. Speaker
The hon. member (Mr. W. F. Maclean^ has already spoken.
I have not spoken on the general subject; I only asked a question.
It is an infraction of the rules
I still say that I am within the rules, Mr. Speaker, as I only asked a question.
The rule is that a member may not speak twice on the same motion.

With all due respect, Mr. Speaker, I submit that asking a Question is not interpreted as making a speech. I shall not occupy the attention of the House for more than a moment. I am an absolute believer in the public ownership of railways in Canada. Therefore, I believe in this country owning and maintaining in the highest efficiency the Intercolonial. I would like to see it extended and improved on the line indicated by the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Rhodes). I take this measure to be a declaration in favour of the acquisition of local lines, and that it will mean an end to the talk and rumours and secret negotiations said to be under way concerning the handing over of the Intercolonial either to the Canadian Pacific or the Canadian Northern. And with this new departure in favour of public ownership, I believe there will come an absence
The hon. member should confine himself to the question he wishes to ask.

I think, Mr. Speaker, I can set myself right in your eyes by explaining that I said I had asked a question only, but had not spoken on the subject. I think I am quite within your previous ruling, having only asked a question, in speaking on the question now. There is a declaration to-day in favour of the extension of the principle of govern-Mr. BLACK.
ment ownership of railways to the wide extent of taking in all or most of the local lines in the provinces where the Intercolonial railway now runs. But if they are to be taken in, they must be taken in on business terms and on reasonable values, end the roads so acquired and the Intercolonial railway itself must be administered from the point of view of business and efficiency and must be absolutely separated from politics. I believe if public ownership is attempted in this country on those lines it will succeed, and I hope that not only will the Intercolonial railway be widened and broadened in the maritime provinces, but that at an early date this state-owned road, which to-day is Canada's greatest asset, will be extended from the Atlantic to the Pacific. I want to see the state-owned road extended into Ontario, I want to see it at the Niagara river and the Detroit river, and most of all I wish to see it extended where there is abundance of traffic and where the competition of such a road would discipline the great private-owned roads, that is in the west. We were told a while ago that it was very much in the air that the Intercolonial railway was to pass into the hands of the Canadian Pacific railway or the Canadian Northern. Instead of the disappearance of that road, I wish to see it extended, its administration made efficient, and its operations extended to the west. If there is room in this country for the extension of the Grand Trunk railway to the Canadian west, there should have been room and there is to-day room for the extension of the state-owned road to the Canadian west. My objection to the Transcontinental system is not so much that it was not required, it was required very much, but that I thought it should have been a part of the present state-owned road, the Intercolonial railway system. The government which is to-day taking the power to lease these roads could a short time ago have taken over the Parry Sound road which the Grand Trunk railway have now acquired. If they had acquired that road on reasonable terms, or on lease, the Intercolonial railway would to-day have been at the Georgian bay, which is now the source of the greatest amount of traffic for the roads going east. The Canadian Pacific railway are now double-tracking their system from the Georgian bay to Montreal and the ports of the St. Lawrence in order that they may handle the traffic of the west. In the same way, if the Intercolonial railway-had taken a lease of the Canada Atlantic, the policy which is now begun in the east where there is very little traffic, -would have produced such results that the Intercolonial railway, the state-owned road, would be in a much better position, would be able to pay all its expenses and even some interest on the cost of construction. So I agree

with the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Rhodes) that the principle is not a bad one, but that it ought to be lived up to in the best way. Speaking of state ownership and taking over leases, one way of bedevilling public ownership, and it has been practised a good deal in this country, is to apply the principle only where there is very little traffic or Business, and then you have public ownership condemned. Take the instance of the government telegraph systems. The only government owned telegraph systems in Canada are those supplying the coast where there is very little or no business, and as a consequence, if you want to cite a horrible example of public ownership, you say: Oh, look at the government telegraph system! The only way to apply government ownership is to apply it where there is business and traffic, and the only way in which the Intercolonial railway will become the success it ought to become is to extend it into the province of Ontario, extend it to the Niagara boundary, to the Detroit river, put it in touch with the Georgian bay and extend it through the great Canadian west. That is the way to work government ownership in this country, and that is the way I hope we will yet see it.

Mr. Speaker, there is no doubt that the taking over of short branch lines connecting with the trunk line is, as a rule a very wise and proper policy. I understand from the Minister of Railways that in connection with the report which he proposed to get from his advisory board, the business aspect of these lines will be considered as well as their physical fitness. If they are taken over on a business basis, there is no doubt it should be a good thing for the branch lines, a good thing for the Intercolonial railway, and a good thing for the country. The danger is that very often branch lines are taken over as feeders and they turn out to be suckers. If that can be avoided I think the principle of the Bill is exceedingly good.

It has been stated this afternoon that this Bill, if passed, will not confer on the government any more power than it has already. That of course may be the case but the Bill is important because it will be, if passed, the adoption by this House of the principle of the Intercolonial railway taking over the branch lines in the maritime provinces. We listened a couple of years ago to a very interesting discourse on this subject by the present member for Westmorland (Mr. Emmerson). He went into the matter very fully and I think gave very good reasons indeed why the branch lines in the maritime provinces should be taken over by the Intercolonial railway. I agreed with the remarks of that hon. gentleman when he made them in this House. I
thought his reasoning was sound and I am prepared to vote for this Bill which gives the Minister of Railways power to go into the taking over of these branch lines under certain favourable conditions. Why, Sir, in the rest of Canada, leaving out the maritime provinces, the uniform policy of the great through lines has been the taking over of branch lines, the building of branch lines, the grid-ironing of the country with their own lines and feeders, and in that way they have succeeded in becoming prosperous and in serving the country to a far greater extent than they otherwise would have done. There can be no doubt that the policy which has succeeded so well in the western part of Canada would succeed equally well in regard to the eastern provinces. I cannot see any reason why this Bill should not pass, especially as, by its adoption, parliament will approve of the principle of taking over these branch lines. I do not support it because the Intel colonial is owned and operated by the gcvernment. I quite agree with those who think that perhaps the Intercolonial railway might have been much better operated and governed under a private owner than it has been under the government. At the same time the Intercolonial railway remains there one of the guarantees of confederation; and I am quite sure that the people of the maritime provinces are determined to keep that line in the ownership of the people of this country. I do not believe that the large majority of the people of the maritime provinces will consent to its passing out of the hands of the people of this country. For these reasons I shall be pleased to vote for the Bill.
Motion agreed to. and House went into committee on the Bill.

As intimated a few minutes ago there is no objection at all to the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) to make clear our intention, except that there is a correction of one clerical error which I have made. I have inserted the word 'chief so as to make it read 'chief engineer.' I propose this amendment to section 3:
