That clause 3 of the Bill be amended by inserting, in the 26th line thereof, after' the word ' Canada ' the words ' nor shall any such connecting railway be entered upon or operated on behalf of the government of Canada until the said managing board and the said chief engineer shall have approved the terms and conditions of such lease having regard to the beneficial results to the government railways and until the parliament of Canada has ratified such lease.
I think the clause would be better drafted if the words Tine or' were inserted between the words 'such' and Tines' in line 20. I therefore beg to move:

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is the committee ready for the amendment proposed by the Minister of Railways and Canals?

That meets the objection that I raised provided the meaning is clear. 'Having regard to the beneficial results to the government railways.' How broad is that? I had a thought like this- may be this carries it out-that the board of managers would write a full report showing that the line of railway in question, from its situation, condition and traffic resources, is one the acquisition of which, under the proposed terms of the lease, will result beneficially to the net revenue of the government railways.
This covers the point.
If it covers it that is what I want. I want a reasoned report.
A report will be required giving reasons.

And showing that good will result to the goverment road from a money point of view.
Amendment (Mr. Graham) agreed to.

That the words ' be binding upon the government of Canada ' in the 26tli line be struck out and instead thereof there be inserted the words ' have any force or effect.'
He said: I suggest this for the reason that the lease is made in the first instance by the Minister of Railways, and I do not see why the proviso should substitute for the minister the government of Canada. I submit that it would be better to use general words and say that no such lease shall have any force or effect until the parliament of Canada has ratified the same.
Amendment agreed to.

In view of the amendment which has been added to the Bill I think it would be safe in striking out the words:	If such lines are reported by the
chief engineer of the Department of Railways to be in a good and safe condition for operation. I can conceive of a railway not being in a good and safe condition for operation, but which it might be advantageous to the country to take over and put in good condition, and operate as part of the system. There are perhaps some lines of railway in New Brunswick of which it might be said that they are not in first-class condition for operation, but which might be taken over and operated very advantageously from the standpoint of the country and of the Intercolonial railway itself. The words added to the Bill: 'Having regard Mr. RHODES.
to the beneficial results to the government railway,' make it possible for us to safely strike out the words I have referred to, and leave the question entirely in the hands of the board and of the engineer. I take it that any proposition of the kind must now be submitted to parliament for approval and that the facts will be stated in regard to the condition of any railway which it may be thought desirable to take over, and therefore it would be just as well to authorize the government to negotiate for the taking over of any branch railway which might be thought advantageous to the government railway system.

I suppose the province of New Brunswick is more interested in this question than any other province because it has a greater number of branches of the Intercolonial than Nova Scotia or Quebec. But while that is so there would be very serious objection to changing the Bill in the way proposed by my hon. friend (Mr. Crocket). It is one of the essential features of this Bill that parliament shall not adopt the principle of entering upon a large capital expenditure in connection with any of these branch railways. One great objection which would be raised in other portions of Canada would be that such a proposition as that set forth by the hon. gentleman might involve the country in a large capital expenditure. The Bill provides that the managing board can only make a recommendation for the leasing of a road when it is certified by the chief engineer that that road is in good and efficient condition for operation as part of the government railway system. That is a safeguard which it seems to me will commend itself to prudent men all over Canada whether they live within the sphere of the influence of the Intercolonial railway or not. It would be very unwise to change the Bill in this respect. If there is a railway which is not at present in good condition and which the board of management may think it desirable to acquire it would not be a very difficult thing for the owners of that road to make the necessary financial arrangements to put it in proper condition, on the assurance that it might then be leased to the government. Of course the rental to be paid by the government upon the recommendation of the board of management would be to some extent based upon the expenditure incurred by the company in bringing the road up to the required standard. If any special case should arise which the board could not deal with under this Act that case could be brought before parliament and considered by itself. It seems to me that in adopting this general principle we ought to be very careful that we do not authorize the Minister of Railways or the managing board to enter into negotiations with respect to any road which


would involve any large capital expenditure, or indeed any capital expenditure at all on the part of the government.

I would agree with the Minister of Public Works if under the terms of this Bill parliament were not to be consulted before any such road was leased. But, when we provide that a Bill shall be submitted to parliament for the leasing of the road it does seem to me that no harm can be done if we authorized the Minister of Railways to negotiate so that even although a road may not at present be such as the engineering department would describe as in good and working condition, that road might advantageously be taken over by the government and put in good condition afterwards. My idea is that if it is intended to take over such a road it would be far better to have the government put it in good condition than to have the railway company do it simply for the purpose of leasing it to the government.

I agree with the remarks of my hon. friend (Mr. Crocket). We have this afternoon adopted this principle largely on the ground that it is the invariable practice of all the big roads to take in the smaller lines and to improve the service and give better facilities to the people. If a road happens to be in bad condition and it would be advantageous for the country to take it, and the owners could not get the money to put it in proper condition, the improved service will not be given to the people and our idea will not be realized. If the principle is sound it ought to be applied to any road which when put in good condition by the government would serve the general public and would be advantageous to the government system of railways.

It seems to me that the principle upon which the government, on the advice of the Railway Board, is to take over any given branch line is the consideration whether that line would be a paying one for the government.
Not that alone.
If that be the principle then we need not object to capital expenditure on these lines if we can get a fair return for our money. I think there is much in the suggestion of my hon. friend from York.

I quite appreciate that hon. gentlemen opposite are now willing to go much further than I contemplated. But, if it is found that this Bill works out in the interests of the people and in the interests of the government railways it would be possible to meet their views later on. However, we must be very careful that the power which we take under this Bill shall meet with the approval of the people
of Canada. There is no use disguising the fact that there has been a good deal of criticism on both sides of the House on the large expenditure of capital on the Intercolonial. In submitting this Bill to parliament I wanted to guard against the criticism which would have at once been launched, that we were opening the door which perhaps might lead to an enormous addition to the capital expenditure on the Intercolonial. It is well to proceed gradually. If we find that the lines that we take over meet with acceptation we perhaps may come to parliament later and change the Act as is suggested. But for the present I want to tie up the Board of Railway Management so that they cannot recommend the acquisition of a line unless it is placed in such a condition that it would not require an immediate large outlay of capital. With that condition, the question of whether it would be profitable or beneficial would be largely problematical. Once started on the expenditure of capital for the improvement of a line, we do not know where that expenditure will end. We merely say to the company, we propose to lease your line if after full investigation we come to the conclusion that if it were put in proper condition it would at least support itself. There is no trouble about a company under such circumstances being able to finance such improvements as would put it into good condition. Thus we avoid opening the door to a large capital expenditure; but if such a door is opened it will not be closed if it turns out to be for the benefit of the country and of the government railway.

While on the subject of the possible cost of improvement to these railways and the expenditure likely to be incurred by the government in acquiring them, I would like to ask the minister if he. has any plan as to the fixing of the basis of rental which would be paid for any roads that might be taken over; whether the amounts which have been paid, either by a provincial government or the Dominion government, in the way of subsidies to aid in the construction of any of these branch lines or connecting roads, will be taken into consideration by him when the rents are determined? I have in mind particularly the case of the Halifax and South Western railway, one of the connecting roads which may possibly receive some benefit under this Bill. The minister, in reply to a question asked by the hon. member for North Grey (Mr. Mid-dlebro), has very frankly stated that, so far as he is aware at the present time, no application has been made by any branch or connecting road to participate in the benefits of this Act. At the same time, from the information which I have been able to obtain from time to time regarding the oper-

ation of the Halifax and South Western railway, and the results of its operations so far as revenue is concerned, I am very much inclined to think that it is not altogether unlikely that in the comparatively near future that railway will be one of those brought under this Act. According to Poor's Manual of Railways, 1908, the government of the Dominion of Canada paid toward the construction of that road, including the Middleton and Victoria Beach branches, the sum of $1,147,069, and the province of Nova Scotia contributed $2,213,173 in subsidy and by way of loan. It has been stated to me, though I am not prepared to say that the information is correct, that the company is not at the present time earning the operating expenses and fixed charges of the road. If that be the case, it is not unlikely that when the door is opened, this company will ask, or possibly the government of Nova Scotia, being the mortgagor, may ask, that the government of Canada enter into arrangements for the leasing of that line. Under these circumstances, I think it might very properly be asked of the minister that he should state to the committee whether he has arrived at any conclusion as to the basis upon which these rentals would be fixed, and as to whether he is in a position to say that the amount of such subsidies which have been paid would be taken into consideration and would in any way lessen the amount of rental which would ordinarily be paid in cases where large subsidies and loans had not obtained.

I have not thought much along that line, but my idea was riveted to this point, outlined in the Bill and the amendment, that the chief thing to be kept in mind is, can we lease this line so that it will be a benefit to the government railway and to the country. The details will all lead to that point. If what my hon. friend says be true, that the Halifax and South Western railway is losing money all the time in its operation, perhaps it would not be up to the standard which the board would require in any line proposed to be taken over. As a matter of fact, I think the Nova Scotia government has a mortgage on the Halifax and South Western railway, and if anything were done with regard to that line-I have no intimation that anything of the kind would be done-it would probably be that the Nova Scotia government would proceed against the railway or would become the interested party. I can assure my hon. friend that his statement is the first intimation that I have had that the Halifax and South Western Railway Company had any idea of leasing their line to the government. But all the questions brought up by my hon. friend will be considered from this point of view: will this road benefit the Mr. JAMESON.
Intercolonial railway and assist the people in the transportation of their products?
And will the terms be reasonable?

Of course.
On the question, that the Bill be reported :

After this lengthened discussion, I feel that I have a very slight knowledge of this Bill, and I think other members are in the same position. I think it a pity that a Bill of such far-reaching importance as this, and cut and slashed in the manner in which this has been, should be dealt with without having some expert draftsmen go over it and make all these clauses fit one into the other. I think the minister would be well advised if he would ask the committee to rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again, and in the meantime have this Bill submitted to the law officers of his department to see if its various clauses are well fitted together.

This Bill was drawn by the legal adviser of my department and was submitted to the law clerk of the House of Commons, and the amendment is that of the hon. member for Hamilton, who is himself a good lawyer and draftsman.
If the hon. minister had allowed the amendment of the hon. member for Hamilton to remain as he suggested it, I would have much more faith in it.
I did exactly.

Was there not an amendment to the amendment? At any rate, the Bill has been amended and reamended so much that I think it should receive the mature consideration of some expert draftsman to see that the different parts properly fit into each other and in such a manner that the Bill will be workable.
Bill reported as amended, and amendments read the first and second time and agreed to.

Mr. GRAHAM moved the second reading of Bill (No. 19) to amend the Intercolonial and Prince Edward Island Railways Employees' Provident Fund Act. He said: As hon. gentlemen know, the Provident Fund Act is an Act under which the employees of the government railways contribute a certain amount, the government duplicates the amount, and on retirement of the employees they get a certain allowance. It is along the lines adopted by

the other great railways of Canada and the United States, and this amendment is designed to make the terms of the Provident Fund Act a trifle more liberal to employees. I will tell the House franklv my object in introducing this Bill. Owing to the large reduction in the staff of the government railwavs, quite a number of the older employees have been for the time being dropped from the service; I would not like to use the term 'dismissed,' because if opportunity offers these will be the first men to be re-employed.
What does the minister mean by employees? Does he mean merely workmen, or does that include railway officers?

It includes some of the railway officers, but some of them are under the old Superannuation Act. The term 'employees' includes the workmen, who are bv far the larger number. Not a few of the older men who have been working on the government railways for many years were dropped. The hardship to them came from the fact that some of them, perhaps from 75 to 100 in number, speaking roughly, were within a few years of the time at which they could have had some benefit from the provident fund, but dropping them at this time Drecluded them from receiving that benefit. The case was represented to me, not pushed at all; but a few months ago a gentleman pointed out that this was a hardship to some of the old employees, and after thinking the matter over I came to the conclusion that, looking at it from the human side, it was a hardship. Men who had worked for a number of years for the government, and contributed to the provident fund a certain amount, and were then dropped out, although in a few years they would have become entitled to the benefit of the fund, that seemed to be a hardship.
Would the minister define what he means by 'a few' years.

Under the present statute, the number of years an employee has to work before he is entitled to be placed unon the provident fund is 15; my Bill proposes to reduce that time to 10 years, and to apply it to those who were in the employ of the government up to March 31 last. My sole object is to meet the situation that has arisen by dropping a lot of these men, and depriving them of the benefit they would have had if they had remained a little longer; in other words, those who were dropped since March 31 last, and have been in the employ of the government for 10 years, can be placed under the provident fund.
Can the minister say whether there are not some men who, on March 31, were within a month or a few days of being entitled to the fund?

The reason we take that arbitrary position is that before that time there were very few men who were dropped except for cause, dismissed absolutely. But here are men who were dropped because the board of management thought the staff was too large, they were not dropped because of any fault of their own.
Are those men now in the service that have been retired?
The men have been dropped. Advisedly I did not use the word 'dismissed,' because it is the intention of the board, if at anv time the services of these men are again required, to re-engage them.
This Act will apply to a few men who may hereafter be retired.
This will apply to a few. It reduces the time, and makes that reduction to all men who were retired since March 31 last.

I would ask the minister to consider a proposition to extend the advantages of that section to men who have been permanently disabled while in the employ of the government but who had not yet served long enough to obtain the advantages of the retirement fund, having served perhans a couple of years short of the 15. I think there ought to be some reasonable limitations to cover that class of men.

The minister says in the second section of the Bill that this amendment should not apply to any person retired prior to the 1st day of April, 1909. What about the persons who were retired between the 1st day of April and the coming into force of this Act?
I think these will be included.
It does not state that it should apply to persons retired between those dates.
We must read into it the consequence that it does apply to any person retired since the 1st day of April of this year. All but those who are executed will be included.
Motion agreed to, Bill read the second time, and House went into committee thereon.

Are the men referred to bv the minister a few minutes ago those who were under investigation recently by Judge Barron, Mr. O'Donaghue and

another? I understand there was an investigation quite recently into the cause of the dismissal of 350 men from the Intercolonial road. Are these the men referred to?

That takes a little explanation. It does not apply to any particular class, but to all employees that come within the scope of the Act. In the case of certain employees, a conciliation board was asked for by the men themselves. A conciliation board was asked for by the men of Halifax, and that conciliation board was formed with Sir George Garneau as chairman. That board made a report a few days ago. This other board, to which the hon. member (Mr. Lennox) refers, was asked for by the men at Moncton who have their own brotherhoods. This board will make a report on the grievances complained of. It may be of interest to hon. members to know that, from the despatch I have just seen in the Toronto papers, the board suggested that this measure should be passed, as it will assist in meeting some of the difficulties that in the *opinion of the board, seem to exist.

That is what I was referring to. These gentlemen recommend that some legislation should be passed that would enable the minister to deal with companies of this kind; and I presume that some of these men dealt with in that report would be covered by this legislation.
Yes, they would.
What was the necessity of appointing this commission consisting of Judge Barron, Mr. O'Donoghue and another? Why did the minister feel called upon to appoint them?
The minister did not feel called upon to appoint them and did not do so.
Who made the appointment?
They were a board of conciliation appointed under the Act, asked for by the men themselves.
Who appointed them?

A board of conciliation, under the Act, is constituted in this manner: When the workmen of the Intercolonial, or any other railway, let us say, think they have a grievance against the management, they ask the Department of Labour to appoint a board of conciliation.
Then, they were appointed by the government?
The men select one member, the management selects another, and if these two do not agree on the third, the appointment of the third is made by the Department of Labour.
Whom did the Department of Labour appoint in this case to this commission?
It is not a commission, but a board of conciliation. And there were two such boards that have been spoken of here; to which does the hon. member (Mr. Hughes) refer?
The one of which Judge Barron and Mr. O'Donoghue were members.
The Department of Labour appointed Judge Barron.

I desire to express my entire disapproval of the minister appointing a board in the manner he has done. No provision is made for the appointment of such a board as sat for the consideration of these matters. The Industrial Disputes Act does not apply to the Crown, in the absence of any specific provision making it so applicable. It seems to me that for the Crown to resort to the provisions of an Act of that kind to settle disputes with its servants is a very unfortunate principle, one that ought not to be acted upon in the Railway Department or any other. Until we have a declaration on the statute-book and some method by which the Act is to be applied, it seems to me that no department of the government should be made a party to such a proceeding.
Do I understand the hon. member (Mr. Macdonald) to say that the Minister of Labour had no right to make the appointment?

My hon. friend (Mr. Crocket) is a member of the legal profession and will appreciate what I said. I ventured the opinion that the Industrial Disputes Act did not apply to any department of the government. That is my position as a lawyer. The hon. member can draw his own conclusions.
Did this appointment purport to be made under the Industrial Disputes Act?
I think we ought to have that point understood. It is a very important one. We should have some explanation.
I suppose this raises the whole question of the Crown's prerogative.
It raises the question of King's prerogative.

It is a very large question, and I do not intend to discuss it. I may be all wrong, but I think that when the Crown goes into running a railway it might conform to all the conditions that govern other people in the same line of business. The employees on the government railway have the same brotherhoods,

the same rules and regulations as the employees of any other road. They would consider it rather arbitrary, if, having provided machinery by which the employees of company roads can ask for boards to settle a grievance, the very authority that created the machinery should refuse the use of that machinery to correct grievances on the government line. Speaking broadly, I suppose, the Crown is not subject to any of these laws. But I am told that when the Industrial Disputes Act was up for discussion in this House, it was generally understood that the employees of the Intercolonial railway should have the same privileges under the Act as the employees of any other railway. As to the legal "part of it, I will leave that out of the question, because the road, during the whole of my time, and, I believe, ever since the introduction of the Industrial Disputes Act, has allowed the employees to apply for a board of conciliation and it has been granted.

But the minister has not touched the point raised by the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. E. M. Macdonald). If it is the policy that boards of conciliation be created in respect of employees of the Intercolonial, the only means by which that can properly be done is by a statute. That is perfectly plain and straightforward. But when you undertake to apply to the employees of the Intercolonial a statute which is not legally applicable, though, of course, the Minister of Railways has not any regard for the legal side of the question -it seems to me a curious
I did not say that.

It seemed to amount t<? that. Of course, there is a great deal of force in what the minister says, that if the Crown carries on business it ought to carry it on under the usual methods. But it is absolutely true, as the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. E. M. Macdonald) has said, that no statute is binding on the Crown unless the Crown is expressly made, subject to the provisions of that statute, and no consensus of opinion of the House of Commons, no expression of that kind in the progress of debate, has any more effect on that statute than the deliberations of any debating society. The difficulty of the situation is that when you are proceeding under a statute which has no application whatever, the whole matter is without any legal foundation, the persons appointed are not properly appointed, they have no right to subpoena witnesses, the witnesses have no right to be paid and any witness can insult the commissioners, disregard their authority, treat them with contempt and nothing -can be done about it. The result would be to bring the whole operation into public contempt of the community upon occasion. That is if my hon. friend from
Pictou is correct in the statement that there is nothing in the statute which makes it binding upon the Crown, and my recollection is the same as his.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: There is some misapprehension, I believe, in the impression derived from the position taken by my hon. friend from Pictou. The Conciliation Act, as I understand it, does not apply to the Intercolonial railway men. The consequence is that the railway employees can refuse to be bound by that Act, they could so on strike with impunity. But in this matter the railway authorities thought it advisable voluntarily to apply to themselves the provisions of the Conciliation Act. They had certain disputes with the management, and it was thought advisable, very properly, to have a conciliation board, to bring themselves under the Act. It was not perhaps legal, but it was voluntary and was acted upon in a voluntary manner. They agreed to have a conciliation, they selected their own arbitrator, the management selected another and these two called upon the Minister of Labour to select a third. All this was done in a voluntary manner. I do not think it was done under the law, but it was done by consent, and the result was the same, a satisfactory conclusion of the dispute between the railway men and the board of management. If the men had refused to be bound by that Act, no authority would have been able to force them to act on it, but of their own motion they chose to come under the provisions of the statute.

Then it is just the same as if some other body of men to whom the Act does not apply had done the same thing? The difficulty is that whenever anyone chooses to treat the court as having no legal position and. for instance, refuses to obey a subpoena or to acknowledge the authority of the court, all the proceedings fall into contempt. Therefore, I say if the Intercolonial railway employees are to have the benefit of this Act, their rights should be given to them by a statute of this country, they should not be dealt with in this way. If it is worth while putting such a provision on the statute-book, and if it is desirable to give it a more extended application, the way to do so is by passing a proper amending Act.

I think you will look in vain for any proceeding where the Crown has abrogated the right to deal with its own servants in whatever way it deems best, and the responsibility of the Crown on the advice of the different ministers to take a certain course in regard to its servants is a matter in regard to which it is responsible to parliament, and the minister's responsibility in such a case cannot be abrogated by saying that a conciliation

board has come to a certain conclusion and therefore the government is rid of the responsibility. Personally, I do not think that in the case of the Intercolonial railway it is wise that the provisions of this Act should apply. These men are servants of the Crown. I know of no case in which they have threatened to strike, or have struck, and I cannot conceive of a case in which they would strike. I think the minister is the proper person to remedy the grievances that exist and to deal with them, and he is responsible to parliament for his course in regard to them. I mention this matter because I not only think there was no legal authority for the appointment of the board, but I think that as a matter of policy the board should not have been appointed.
Why not change the reading of clause (f) to make it apply to those who were in the service on the 1st day of April, 1909?

The law clerk of the House advises me that that clause refers to the original Act and this amendment is passed as if it were part of the original Act. Therefore, the form used is necessary.
At six o'clock, House took recess.
After Recess.
House resumed at eight o'clock.

I observe that this fund is provided, one half by the government and one half by the monthly contributions of the employees of the Intercolonial railway and the Prince Edward Island railway. The fund is to be administered by a board consisting of five persons, of whom one is the general manager of the Intercolonial railway, who shall be the chairman and preside at meetings of the board; two members appointed by the minister from among the chief officers of the railway, one of whom shall always act as chairman in the absence of the general manager and the remaining two shall be elected annually by the employees contributing to the fund. I would like to know whether the proposed amendment has been submitted to the board or the representatives of the employees who contribute half the amount of the fund and, if not, whether the minister does not think it would be fair to give them an opportunity of being heard.

I have received a communication, not in reference to this, but in reference to some other things that the employees want to place before me. There is no doubt in the world about them being in harmony with this Bill, I think, but they are going to submit some other matters to me early in January. I thought that if we put this Bill through the committee stage I would let it stand for the third reading, Mr. E. M. MACDONALD.
and then, if there is anything that they desire by way of amendment, it can be dealt with before the Bill receives its third reading. There is a committee representing the men who were on the provident fund, or those who were interested, and I will ask them to present to me in writing the matters which they desire to bring to my attention so that I can submit their proposals to the board before we assemble again after recess. I expect that will be done.

Of course, I am quite prepared to accept the assurance of the minister that they are entirely in harmony with the proposals, but at the same time I do not see how they can be in harmony with them if they da not know anything about them; nor do I see how the minister can be sure that they are in harmony with them if he has not heard anything from them. That, however, is a matter for himself and the committee will be bound to accept his assurance. I am under the impression that the minister added to the rules of the fund a note to "the following effect:
No absolute right of retirement exists under this Act. It must he clearly understood that the fund is a provident fund for the purpose of caring for disabled, worn out and old employees and not a retiring fund for the purpose of allowing men to secure other employment and at the same time draw an allowance.
I understood that that was the memorandum of the minister and I am not sure that it met the approval of the board. The minister will know about that. Does the minister consider that the proposal contained in clause (f) is quite in harmony with this note, for which he, I understand, is responsible.

I am not responsible for that note, but the object of that was to prevent applications being made by men for retirement who really left the employment of the road to better themselves. We have had men who left their employment whom the board did not consider as being entitled to be put on the provident fund at all. No man may. demand to go on the provident fund. He may make his application and that application is referred to the board, which is composed of the representatives of the men as well as of the government, each furnishing a portion of the money for the purpose. That board, after taking into consideration all the circumstances, pass upon the application before it comes to the minister. Then, it comes to the minister for his approval, and I think that no injustice can be done to any person. Some circumstances have arisen in which men have.no right to the benefits of the retirement, fund, because they took other employment and simply

wished to better their positions. They endeavoured to get their retirement allowance and to better their position at the same time.
It will still be necessary to secure the recommendation of the board in order to be placed on the fund?
Yes, absolutely.
That provision is not interfered with in any way?
Not at all.
I do not think the minister has mentioned how many people will probably come within the scope of this Act.
Yes.
About how many?

The chairman of the board told me that he thought between 75 and 100. It is a little difficult to say because we have not the ages of the 'men, but from the information he received he thought the number would not be more than 100.

Some reference has been made to the conciliation boards. We have had two conciliation boards. The last conciliation board which was referred to this afternoon was a board called together for the purpose of ascertaining the rights of some men who had been dismissed from the Intercolonial railway within the last year. I think that is what they were called together for.
That was one of the questions before the board.	.
Has it anything to do with this Bill?
No.
Because if it has I would like to bring up some other matters in connection with it.
The minister said that it had to do with it, that a number of the men who had been dismissed and whose case was investigated would, with others, come within the scope of this Bill.

The board itself would not have anything to do with this Bill. Any person whose services were dispensed with w'ould come under this arrangement, whether they were in that class or some other class. They would be affected by this Bill, but the conciliation board itself would have nothing to do with it.

Then, if I understand it, the Bill is intended only to apply to employees from April, 1909? It does not go any further back than that? These men
who have had this conciliation board dealing with their affairs certainly were dismissed. They were all out of employment before that time and consequently this Bill would not cover them.

One of the things for which the employees asked for the conciliation board was to ascertain if the management of the road had not violated some agreement with them in dispensing with the services of several of them since April 1 last, because that is when the board took charge. This Bill deals with the employees who were dismissed since April 1, 1909, and any man of them who had then served ten years would be entitled to superannuation if the board recommends it. Without this amendment he could not be superannuated unless he had served fifteen years.
Is there any restriction as to the age of the employees who will be entitled to the advantages of this section?
It only applies to men who are seventy years of age and have been ten years in the service, we substitute ten years for fifteen.

Yes, but are you not making provision for another class of people who no matter what their age, were removed since April the 1st, 1899. Under the wording of this would they be entitled to superannuation ?
They have to fulfil all the other conditions.
Yes, but there are different classes mentioned and in all these classes an age limit is specified and now you are adding an additional section in which there is no age limit.

I should think that the point mentioned by my hon. friend (Mr. .Macdonald) is well taken. I am not discussing the question of policy but simply the construction of the statute, and if the clause is passed as it now reads there would be no age limit stipulated.

I think the point is well taken. Under the old Act m6n who withdrew from the service for any reason would not participate in the provident fund until they had reached 60 years, and I do not think we would be doing any injustice if we put the age limit here at 55 years, then they would have the benefit of five years in the two rvays.
What is the object of restricting this Act to those who are retired since April the 1st 1909?

Before that date there were practically few compulsory retirements except for cause, and a man who was dis-

missed for cause would not have any claim on the provident fund. But since April the 1st the board has dispensed with a large number of men whose only fault was that they were not required in the service. By this legislation I am trying to meet the well .founded complaint that they were harshly dealt with.
Does the minister say that men were not dismissed before April, 1909?
I would not say that, but as a rule the men retired before that time were retired for some cause.
Political or otherwise.
No.
How many men have dropped from the service since April the 1st last?
I gave the number in ' Hansard ' the other day; I think about 500.

I understand that there were quite a number of men dismissed and particularly in Halifax, between the 1st of December, 1908, and April, 1909, and some of these were men who had served 25 years but who not having reached the age limit of 60 years were not provided for out of the provident fund. They were dismissed simply because their services were not required.
I have not had any cases of that kind brought to my notice.

If there are cases of that kind would it not be very unjust to provide for those whose services were dispensed with since April, while you make no provision for those who were dropped between December and April.
If there are such cases I imagine that the committee which is to wait on me will probably present them. We will not press the Bill to the third reading until we hear from that delegation.
I should think that would be satisfactory. One class of employees should be provided for as well as the other.
We are to understand then definitely that the Bill will not be read a third time until this delegation makes its views known to the minister.
Yes.
Would it not be better to leave the Bill in committee?
We can refer it back to committee if there is any difficulty.

It is much better to leave it in committee. There is a great deal in what has been said by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Crosby). Here we Mr. GRAHAM.
have men who have not been in the service for more than 10 years who are being dismissed, which is proof of what we have contended often from this side of the House that we have had a small army of men on that railroad who were not required at all. If it is fair and equitable-and I am not going to object to it, because I have a good deal of sympathy with the men-to make compensation to those men who have been in the service only 10 years, many of whom admittedly should not have been in the service at all, would it not be far more equitable to make provision for men who have been probably 25 years in the service, and yet have not reached the age of 60 years? I think it is pretty harsh that a man who is 59 years of age and has been say 25 years in the service, is to get no consideration at all. When we are reconsidering the Act, let us reconsider fully, and do justice all round. The question arises from the fact that we have had a large number of people employed on the railway who should never have been employed there at all. This is no fault of these men, though a great deal of fault to the government, and I am disposed to treat these men generously, or at all events justly. We shall not be doing even-handed justice if we do not consider the cases of the men who have almost reached the age limit. I do not think the minister should object to leave the Bill in the committee for fuller investigation.

Let us understand clearly what we are talking about. In the first section the wording of the Bill is: 'Those who are in the service at the time of the coming into force of this Act'. As I understand the minister, those words do not mean at the time of the coming into force of this Bill as an Act, but they mean those who were in the service on the 22nd of March, 1907.
That is correct.

I think perhaps the minister w'ould have avoided some confusion if, instead of saying 'at the time of the coming into force of this Act', he had said, on the 22nd of March, 1907, which is the date he is referring to.

I had not the Bill drafted in this way originally, but on being referred to the law clerk of the House of Commons, he redrafted it in this form in order to keep it within the four corners of the original Act.
There was no objection to the words 'the 22nd of March, 1907', in the original Act, and if they were put into this Bill there would be no confusion.

I think the first section is perfectly clear as it is. It. is incorporated in the original Act and is to be construed as if it had been there when the

Act was originally passed. Therefore the date is when the Act was originally passed.

The Act referred to is the original Act, and this section becomes part of that Act. I wish to move to add the following words at the end of the section 'and had at the time of such retirement reached the age of 55 years'.
Perhaps the minister will explain a little more fully why he is adding those words. He mentions a specific age, which might 'cause a good deal of injustice.

My hon. friend will see that had the old Act remained, only those persons who had reached the age of 60 years could be retired. We are reducing the length of time they have to be in the service by five years, and we are also reducing * the age limit by five years.

At the same time, this Act is intended to apply to only a few men- those who are relieved of duty after the first of April, 1909. That appears to me to be an extremely arbitrary arrangement. 1 think section 2 had better be allowed to stand until this whole matter can be considered again. I do not think the committee has sufficient information to be able to deal with this matter in a proper and judicial way.

This affords an additional reason why this Bill should remain in committee. I understand that a deputation of parties who are interested is going to wait on the minister. I understand from a newspaper report to-day that there has been forwarded to the Minister of Labour a report and recommendation from the recent conciliation board with reference to 350 men. We shall have this deputation waiting on tire minister, and yet not have afforded, up to this moment, any of the men interested any notice whatever that we propose to put a time limit on this provision. The Act has been announced in the press, the men interested know something of it, they understand it to be an Act providing that any man who has been ten years in the service will be entitled to recovery. Now we propose to make an age limit of 55 years. The minister may be right in that or wrong, but the men interested have had no opportunity to present their case. Why amend these sections now when in all probability we ishall have to refer the Bill back to the committee for reconsideration in a few days? Will it not be more sensible to leave the Act unamended, report progress and ask leave to sit again, and leave the Bill in committee?
It is not worth while arguing about it. What I want is to get the measure advanced a stage, and the interests concerned will be protected just the same as under my hon. friend's suggestion.
Except if we determine on 55 years, whether right or wrong, it will be more difficult to alter it afterwards.

It will not make a whit of difference. I do not want to urge the Bill through, but merely as a matter of expedition to get it off the Order Paper, after giving the assurance that I would have it referred back to the committee if necessary. When my hon. friend starts to make out. a case, he must see that no matter what limit we may fix, it would be open to question. There must be a line-drawn somewhere. The Act is arbitrary, and I am just changing the terms a little to meet the condition of the people referred to and who may have some reason for complaining. When the Act was passed, the argument of my hon. friend could have been used just as well as to-day. Section (a) provides:
Those who have attained the age of 70 years after being 15 years in the service.
Why, according to the hon. gentleman's argument, exclude those who were in the service fourteen years and six months? Why exclude people who were fourteen years in office and let in those who were fifteen? You have to draw the line somewhere and make an arbitrary ruling, and any Act to help a certain class of men will give reason for others to complain because they are not included. Take another class, class (b) which covers those, who, after being fifteen years in the service, become physically or mentally incapacitated. But here is a poor man who was fourteen years in the service when he became incapable. Why do injustice to him by excluding him? Take the other class:
Those who have attained the age of 60 years after being 15 years in the service, and request to be retired from the service.
Why not include those who served 13 or 14 years? While there may be something in the contention of my hon. friend, draw the line where you like, it must be arbitrary, and some will come just short of meeting the conditions you impose, no matter how lenient.

We may as well be quite frank in discussing these things. There is an impression, rightly or wrongly, among some people, that men have been dismissed otherwise than for lawful cause, and that possibly some of these clauses may affect the rights of such men. There would not be any difficulty about the first part of section (1). The difficulty seems to be about section (2); and I propose to discuss section (2) with relation only to these 55-year men, leaving the other to be discussed separately. Why not make paragraph (2) read:
The paragraph added to section 12 of the said Act by section 1 of this Act shall not ap-

ply to anybody retired prior to the 1st April, 1909, otherwise than for lawful cause.
This cannot affect the hon. gentleman, as he knows he has not dismissed anybody except for lawful cause.

I am not trying to open the door for a great many years back, but to meet the complaint which has arisen among a large number of the men who have been dismissed by the board. There was no complaint along that line, so far as I have heard, previous to the establishment of the Railway Managing Board. Rightly or wrongly, they have dispensed with the services of many men, and both sides of politics have complained to me that they thought the action of the board was perhaps not wrong in dispensing with the services of these men, but there was quite a number whose services were dispensed with through no fault of their own. This is to meet the conditions which have arisen since the board took charge and dispensed with the services of a large number of men.

I believe this measure is particularly intended to relieve 75 or 100 people who have complied with the conditions of ten-year service. But what will happen the other 350 who have given good service during 4 to 9 years and have been put out in the cold without an hour's notice?

The Provident Funds Act was passed to relieve those who had attained a certain age and men could not be employed, since that Act came into force, over 35 years of age. In the case of men who were employed fairly young and had not served the railway ten years, of course their claim on that fund is not so strong as that of those who have attained a certain age. No one regrets more than I that men should lose their positions. That part of the management of the road has worried my mind more than any other, but in all great industrial enterprises that occurs, and fewer have lost positions on the Intercolonial railway than on any other railway during the last five years.

The hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) suggests that there is less reason for pensioning a man who has been improperly employed for ten years and who has been a charge upon the public funds than one so employed for lesser number of years. There is logic in that, as -the minister must see. The whole thing comes back to this-that the difficulty arises through the fact that the government would not take any action until this Railway Managing Board was appointed. The Managing Board now has discharged men who ought never to have been employed. The fact that these men have been employed ten years rather than five is not a Mr. BARKER.
very logical reason why they should get a pension rather than the five-year men. At the same time, no doubt, it would be a hardship on the men, and I suppose we should have to let it go in the end. It arises from having too many men on the railway.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is section I amended as agreed to?
No, the minister said he would allow it to stand.
If the hon. member (Mr. Lennox) does not wish to carry out the arrangement made between his leader and myself. I am quite willing that it should remain in committee.
I did not understand that any arrangement was made.
The hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) was satisfied that I should leave it until the third reading.
I would not have made objection had I understood that. But I hold to what I said.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is the committee ready for the amendment to section 1 ?
No.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Carried.
I would like to get the Bill into shape so that it can be reprinted, for I propose to send a copy to this committee for their consideration as well as to ask them to send me their suggestions.
And the whole Bill will be open for consideration?
And leave it to the third reading.

We have settled this matter. If we are going to argue further, let us argue it all. If the minister is not prepared to do what he suggested a few minutes ago, there are many things we can discuss) I understood that the minister was ready to move that the committee report progress.

As far as I am concerned, it does not make any difference to me. I submitted the matter to the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) and the gentlemen from the section particularly affected who will probably be waited on by those concerned. If I can get this through to the third reading, I will have it reprinted and a copy sent to the committee. If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lennox) does not want it that way, I am not particular.
That can be done without it going through Committee of the Whole.
It will not be printed unless it passes the committee.
If the minister says he will, on request, send it back to the Committee of the Whole, I think that covers the point.

If my .leader says that he is satisfied with the. proposal, I will certainly submit. At the same time, I do not feel that that is the best way, and I will give my reason:	There are a good many
things in connection with this Bill that we shall want to discuss more at length, and it is advisable that we should have the fullest information before we discuss them. It is not advisable that we should discuss them piecemeal and from time to time. If this Bill remains in committee we should have an opportunity to bring them forward. I submit to the judgment of my leader that it would be better to leave the Bill in committee.

Of course, I do not wish to force my views on any hon. member. But I understand the minister to say that he-desires to get the Bill out of committee that he may have it printed. And he undertakes, on the request of any hon. member, to send it back to the committee after it is reprinted.
Certainly-no trouble.
So, we have only to make the request and we should be where we are now.

As I plainly see that my leader thinks that the proper course, I certainly take his suggestion, and allow the matter to go.
On section 2:
The paragraph added to section 12 of the said Act by section 1 of this Act shall not apply to any person retired prior to the first day of April, one thousand nine hundred and nine.
What objection would there be to striking out this section altogether and allowing this measure to apply from the passage of the Bill of 1907?

That would open up the whole Act very much more than is intended. It would be popular, I have no doubt, but I have no idea what it would cost the country or how much it would cost the men. On the basis of the present section, we have a pretty good idea of how many men would come under it. That matter will be discussed with the representatives of the men when they come.	[DOT]

The hon. minister stated that there had been no dismissals except for cause. So, I thought there could be no objection to striking out this section. I ask it for the sake of those cases, if there 37
are any, that the minister does not call to mind and to whom injustice may have been done and who would be cut out by this paragraph.

The Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) as head of the department knows the position of the employees prior to April, 19u7. If there have been no dismissals prior to that, the elimination of this section will not enlarge the scope of the Act or increase the expenditure necessary to carry it into effect. The hon. minister knows who has been dismissed, and whether dismissed for cause or not. I think the point taken by the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Daniel) is well taken.

If the hon. member (Mr. Samuel Sharpe) had the responsibility of carrying out such an Act and realized the scope of it he would not, I am inclined to think, make the remarks he has made. The men were under certain conditions up to the introduction of this amendment, that is up to April 1, 1909. A new system of management was introduced. The hon. gentleman must remember that there are, if I recall the number correctly, some 8,000 employees on the government railways. If we open the door for those back to 1907 some hon. member may say, ' Why 1907? Let us go back further.' There must be a line, and it must be, in a measure, arbitrary. This Act was passed in 1907. I was not here then, but no doubt many hon. members before me were here at that time. The line was drawn strongly and arbitrarily and an age limit fixed. All I pretend to be attempting to do is to make the Act a little more lenient owing to the new conditions having arisen by the change in management. My hon. friend suggests that I know just who were dismissed out of all these men. I suppose he is not serious in that.
The minister would know the number.

The minister stated there
were none.
I did not state anything of the kind.
Except for cause.

I said once or twice that I did not make that statement, but my hon. friend has put it in my mouth twice since. Generally speaking, before this A t men were dismissed for cause as they would be in any railway or any other line. But when the management was changed the conditions changed, the circumstances to which the old Act applied were altered and a general reduction of the staff all over the system was entered upon. New conditions! arose which acquired a new [DOT] Act. I am trying to meet the conditions



that have arisen owing to a large number of men having been dismissed at once by the board of management. It must be remembered that the men still in the employ of the road will have to pay their share to those men who retire, and this Act has met with their approval. I do not know why in attempting to meet new conditions we should drag in all the old conditions existing before the passage of the Act of 1907. My only attempt was to meet the new conditions that have arisen since the board was appointed.
How many men have been dismissed from October last to the 1st of April?
I think I gave that information in answer to a question.

Information of that kind was given in answer to a question of mine, but it related only to the county of Halifax. When the Bill is again in committee perhaps the minister would be good enough to have all this information ready so that we can discuss it a little more intelligently.
Bill reported.

' go into Committee of Supply.

send a special engineer, but I will again look carefully into the report. My hon. friend also mentioned Battery Point, Digby, Nova Scotia. I find that a part of it belongs to the Department of Militia and Defence and the other part to the Dominion Atlantic Railway Company. Therefore, there is no obligation on my department to make any improvements.

speakeroldname: Hon. WM. PUGSLEY (Minister of Public Works).
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as my hon. friend (Mr. U. Wilson) has mentioned the subject of the dredging of the Napanee river and has intimated that one of the captains has made the statement that navigation is more dangerous than before, I think perhaps I should call the attention of the House to what has actually been done during the past season. Before doing so I may say that before we began working upon that river during the past season the river, for seven miles, was full of obstructions, such as sunken logs and stumps. There was also a wreck right in the channel of the river and it was a serious menace to navigation. It was reported to me, not only by my hon. friend but also by prominent citizens of

Napanee, by captains of vessels as well, that the dredging of this river was necessary in order to give satisfactory navigation. Well, Sir, it is true, as I told my hon. friend and a number of other gentlemen in Napanee, who communicated with me upon this subject, that there was no special appropriation made at the last session of parliament for this work, but I stated that if possible I would endeavour to get a dredge and have the work done. We had no government dredge available for the purpose because our dredges were all busily engaged elsewhere, but we did succeed in making a very satisfactory arrangement with the Windsor Dredging Company, what I think every one who is familiar with the condition of affairs in that river will say was a satisfactory arrangement, the price being 14 cents per cubic yard with a special allowance of $150 for removing the wreck. The report which I have is that dredging has been performed to a depth of 12 feet below low water at various points in the river where most required, the cuts were widened from 25 to 30 feet and the remains of the old wreck were entirely removed. Altogether during the past season this company dredged some 20,000 cubic yards of material in addition to removing the wreck. The total expenditure has been in the vicinity of $2,800. I think from this report and from what I have heard outside of the report the work which has been done has been very satisfactory and excellent value has been got for the money which has been expended I may say to my hon. friend that the question of continuing the dredging will receive careful consideration, but I do trust that my hon. friend recognizes, that, at his own request and at the urgent request of a number of prominent citizens of Napanee, I made arrangements under considerable difficulty to do this work, believing that it was a justifiable work, just as all other work which is done by my department is justifiable work and necessary in the public interest. I can assure my hon. friend that he would make a stronger case for the dredging of the Napanee river if he would simply rely upon the merits of the work which we have on hand and not seek to disparage the public work which is being done in other places. I think it is a great mistake, when one desires that some work should be done in his own locality, that he should feel it necessary to throw out the suggestion that every expenditure made in any other part of the country is a waste of money and that the only place in the whole Dominion of Canada where money can be expended to public advantage is in the particular locality in which he resides.

I did not throw out any such insinuation, I did not intend to a x ^ think, Mr. Speaker, you will bear me out when I say that I gave the minister full 37i
credit for his generosity last year. I acknowledge that under difficulties he made this appropriation. I have a letter from Captain Christie which bears out everything I have said in reference to the dredging. I will let the minister see it.
