speechtext:
This is for the purpose of exbreakwater at Pinckney Point, the difficulty which we are seeking to obviate there is that silt and gravel wash away through the action of the sea and obstruct the berth. We find it necessary to build an extension of the block 40 feet long, the whole cost of which will be $1,000.
Piper's Cove-breakwater-pier, $8,000.

This is to provide for the construction of a breakwater pier at Piper's cove on the Bras D'Or lake; The proposed structure will extend to eight feet at low water, and it proposed to construct blocks and spans 224 feet in length. There is to be a road bridge 270 feet long as well. The total cost is $8,000.
Will this work be done by tender and contract P
Yes, I think this will be done by public tender and contract.

I would like to urge upon the minister the advisability, where-ever possible, of having these works done by contract. There is a variety of very good reasons why this course is preferable to the alternative of having the work done by day labour. ''In most of these communities there is a large number of people who are very anxious to secure employment upon these public works at certain times of the year when they have not very much to do and when it is a great boon to them to be able to make a few dollars. It very often happens that when a work is done by day labour only the personal friends of those who have the management or control of it are placed upon the work, and others, who are equally deserving, are debarred from that privilege. There is another reason why it is desirable to have this work done by contract and that is that it reduces the number of foremen, sub-foremen, supervisers and officials of that character, and saves expense. The cost of construction is lessened, perhaps I may say the cost of officials who do not work is lessened, and a saving is thereby effected to the department. I have found in my own constituency that where the work is done by day labour and not by contract, the privilege of supplying timber and other materials is usually given only to a few individuals who are often compelled

to take the value of the material, out of the store of the person who has charge of the work. In like manner the workmen are obliged to take out theif wages under what is called the truck system. For these reasons it is desirable that the work should be done by contract wherever possible so that all may have a fair chance of participating in the distribution of the money. When work is let by contract this truck system is broken up and that in itself is a good thing. When we were considering the [DOT]other day the appropriation for David's . nove in Digby county I expressed the desire that the work should, if possible, be [DOT]done by contract, and I urged it because the experienoe in that county at least has been that very great hardship has been entailed in the nast on the workingmen and on those who supplied materials in that they had not been able to draw their pay in cash but were frequently compelled to draw it through the shop of the man in [DOT]charge of the work. I know _ that the minister has the welfare of his department and of the public works of Canada at beart, and it is for this reason that I bring this to his attention.

I have already stated that it was the rule of the department to [DOT]do work by contract except in cases where it clearly appeared to the responsible officers that it could be done better by day work. With regard to workmen being [DOT]obliged to take goods from a store in lieu of their pay I wish to state publicly that no foreman has the right to require a man to take his pay otherwise than in cash, and if any complaint is made to the department that a foreman has required those under him to resort to the truck system that foreman would be reprimanded and unless a satisfactory explanation is given,he would be dismissed. Of course it may happen sometimes that workmen in anticipation of a cheque coming for their wages desire to [DOT]obtain supplies in advance from a store, but in all cases it is the well understood duty of the foreman to pay promptly in cash when the money is available in the hands of the engineer.

I may say for the information of the minister that I know a case in which men who are willing to work and who had applied for work were flatly told that unless they took their wages out of the store of the man who had charge of the work he would not give them employment, and, those who were willing to supply material were told that they would have to take their payment in a similar way in respect to this particular work. I think that is a very serious hardship.

Would my hon. friend [DOT]object to giving me the name of the foreman who made that condition and if he does I assure him that I will have the mat-Mr. JAMESON.
ter investigated and will see that such a foreman will not receive further employment. Any foreman who insists upon that condition of employment is certainly not discharging his duty.
I will have great pleasure in giving to the minister privately the name of the foreman.
That will do.
I do not suppose it is necessary to publish the name in ' Hansard ' but I shall give the name to him privately.
Very well.

The view taken by the Minister of Public Works is the proper one and I was quite confident he would take such a view when the matter was brought to his notice. Let me say that if foremen generally have notice from the department that such conduct would not be recognized it would go far towards effecting a cure of this pernicious system.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I like the contract system best, but I am bound to say that I am not so satisfied as my hon. friend (Mr. Jameson) as to its popularity in any given district. I do not say that because it is unpopular it should not be adopted but there are views that may be offered on the other side. The contractor may come from a distant part of the country and very often he brings with him his staff and some of his employees to the exclusion of those living in the neighbourhood, a thing which is never very popular. Then again it sometimes happens that the contractor not having sufficient resources gets into difficulties, and I have known cases where the contractors went away leaving claims unpaid and very much discontent. The contract system, as a rule, is the better one, but there is another side to the question.

If a contractor should bring from outside a considerable portion of the labour to be employed I can well understand that it would not be satisfactory, but in the case of these works ranging from $7,000 to $8,000 I think the contractor would be very likely to find sufficient local iaoour and would not import any. As to a contractor leaving the workingmen unpaid I do not think there is any excuse whatever for such a condition, because it would be a proof that the officers of the department, who had the money in their hands had not exercised proper supervision and had been derelict in their duty.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No. I could give my hon. friend a case where no one was at fault; where the contractor took his work at too low a price and although his intentions were honest enough he got into difficulties and he was not able to pay the workmen. The usual percentage was kept

back but that did not suffice. He was a man of honest purpose but there was not enough money to give him his contract price and a fair profit.
That would be an exceptional case.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes.
Port Dufierin - breakwater at Smiley's Point, $2,550.
This will complete the work.
What is the total cost?
Porter's Lake-boat channel to Three-Fathom harbour, $4,500.
This is an important work, Porter's lake being 17 miles in length and surrounded toy a good farming country, well settled. The total cost of the work, including breakwater, will be $17,000.
Where is this?
In Halifax county. There have been expenditures in 1907-8 and 1908-9.
How much more will toe required to complete the work?
It is estimated that it will take $10,000 more.

As the minister states, this is in a very fertile part of the county of Halifax, and the work gives access to a very beautiful lake. I suppose it is intended that the work shall be continued during the coming summer?

Yes.
Port Hood harbour-closing northern entrance, $40,000.

This is a very important work. A good deal of coal is shipped from Port Hood. Formerly there was a natural breakwater extending from the island to the mainland, tout some years ago it was carried away by a violent storm, and we have been for some years gradually closing the entrance so that it will afford a sheltered harbour. We are asking this year for a larger vote than usual, with a view to proceeding vigorously with the work.
How much has been expended on this work, and what does the minister estimate the total expenditure will be? Also, what material is used in the construction of the breakwater?

The material used has been brush and stone. The total estimated cost was originally $215,000. The work has been carried on continuously since 1903. There has been expended $92,796.67, and with this $40,000 it is estimated that $82,250 will still be required to complete the
work. I may say that this work has been asked for not only by the people of the locality, but by resolutions of various boards of trade, including the Maritime Board of Trade, which has urged the importance of continuing the work as rapidly as possible.

We are frequently told of wharfs being washed away on the Atlantic coast. Is it not possible to devise' some method of constructing these wharfs so that this will not happen so frequently? There must be some fault in construction-

What was washed away was the natural connection between the island and the mainland-not an artificial structure, but a natural breakwater or bar, and the fact of its being washed away deprived the harbour of its natural shelter, and it is for that reason that we are erecting a breakwater.
I may have misunderstood the hon. minister in this case, but all the same we do have constantly recurring cases of wharfs being washed away.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think it often happens that a wharf is washed away. Undoubtedly wharfs are damaged from time to time, and I am afraid that my hon. friend is not sufficiently acquainted with the force of the Atlantic waves, or he would not see anything surprising in that. I am not sure that even concrete works would withstand some of the storms on the Atlantic coast.

I want to call the minister's attention to the fact that while large sums are being expended on wharfs and breakwaters along the coasts of the maritime provinces, some expenditures are necessary on the inland waters. I have had occasion to refer to the need of a little dredging near Wolfe island. The people there build their own wharfs, but in the latter part of last session I informed the minister that an expenditure of $150 or $200 in dredging would enable vessels to land coal on the island, whereas otherwise the people would be obliged to haul their coal on the ice from Kingston. This would mean a saving of fifty or sixty cents a ton on all the coal used on Wolfe island. I simply want to draw attention to that. The hon. minister said last session that it was then too late to consider the matter. I want now to call his attention to it before it is loo late. This is a matter of great importance to the people there, and while we are making these large expenditures down by the sea, we should not forget the people living along the lakes.

The hon. gentleman is speaking of dredging required at Wolfe island. The result of the inquiry I made is

that this is a private wharf, owned by a company, and the business down there is the business of this company, and the work could not be properly regarded as work for the general benefit of the public.

The wharf, I believe, was constructed by private parties who were living on the island, but it is used by the general public without charge. I can only repeat that the dredging would result in great and general benefit to the people on that island inasmuch as it would enable coal vessels to land cargoes there, and the people would then get their coal at 50 cents to 60 cents a ton less.

If the hon. gentleman would write me a letter stating the number of people accommodated by that wharf and mentioning the fact that the wharf is open to public use without charge, I shall be glad to take a note of it for further consideration.
1 200 EDWARDS. The population is some
How long has this work been in progress?
Since 1903.

This is for an extension.
Port Malcolm-wharf, $2,500.

This is to reconstruct. There is a private wharf there now, owned bv Mr. Malcolm. The department is going to acquire that for some $2,100, including the right of way. The department will make it a public wharf and reconstruct it. The total estimated cost, including cost of the property, will be $7,000. I am now asking $2,500 and will require a further $2,500 to complete the reconstruction.
What are the dimensions of the wharf the department is buying?

225 feet in length and it extends to 6i feet below water. For a distance of 105 feet it is 64 feet wide; for a distance of 24 feet, 42 feet wide; for a distance of 70 feet, 18 feet wide; and for the remaining distance of 26 feet, 22 feet wide. That is the existing wharf. We propose to reconstruct it.
How was this figure arrived at? Was that just the amount asked or was an officer of the department sent to examine the wharf?
When will it be completed?
It is proposed to let the contract now and we hope to finish it in about two more years.
When the work was begun in 1903, how is it the department is only giving a contract now?

The work was experimental. To have made a solid breakwater of crib-work and stone would have cost a great deal more perhaps than we felt justified in spending. This mode of construction was an experiment and we went along gradually to see whether it would stand the action of the waves. It has certainly stood remarkably well, and the department is convinced it will be permanent, so that we feel justified in asking a larger appropriation with the view of entering into a contract.
The resident engineer, Mr. Bernard Sconi was instructed to make an examination and report, and he estimated its value at $2,100. It is on his report that we propose to buy the property.
Has the deed been executed?

No, we could not take a deed until we got the vote.
Mr. CROCKET, it?
How large a place is
It has a population of 600; the residents are farmers, who engage in fishing during the fishing season. There is a freight and passenger steamer which calls there.
What county?
Richmond.
If this wharf belongs to a private individual why should the government acquire it?
All that was done by day labour?

Yes.
Mr. CROCKET What is the estimate oi the work yet to be done?
$122,250 to finish the whole work.

The parties who own the wharf are out of business. They conducted a large mercantile establishment there until a few years ago. The senior member of the firm died, and the property is in the market. Up to the present it has been used by the public without charge, but the wharf is not in proper condition at present and a request was made to the department to furnish a new one.
Port Joly-extension of Herring Rocks Mr- CL TAYLOR. We have hundreds of breakwater, $2,000.	cases throughout Ontario of wharfs owned

by private parties and used by the public. We have three or four at Gananoque which the owners would be glad to sell to the government if the government feel disposed to buy old wharfs. I do not see why the government should furnish a wharf at this place.

In Ontario the department has done that frequently. It sometimes happens that a private wharf, owing to the owner having gone out of business, becomes neglected, and there is a justifiable demand for a public wharf. It is often considered best, that, instead of building another wharf, the private wharf should be taken over, where it can be had at a fair and reasonable price, and repaired and devoted to the public use. It has been done in several cases in the province of Ontario and in Quebec also. It is not confined to the province of Nova Scotia, I can assure my hon. friend.
Is this engineer, Bernard Sconi, one of the regular men?
Yes.
In Halifax?
No, in Antigonish.

I would call attention to the wharf at Wolfe Island to which I have already referred. In view of what the minister has said in regard to the policy of acquiring wharfs owned by private individuals who have gone out of mercantile business-

Perhaps the hon. member (Mr. Edwards) will pardon me a suggestion. If he wishes to make a suggestion as to the government acquiring a wharf in Ontario, perhaps it might be more convenient to wait until the Ontario items are before the committee.
If the minister prefers it. It struck me that it would be cheaper for the people if the government will buy the wharf. It could be got for less money than is being paid for this one.
By whom was the department asked to buy this wharf? Was there any request from the municipality?

My hon. friend from Richmond (Mr. Kyte) informs me that he presented a petition of the people urging strongly that this wharf should be acquired. I do not recollect the petition at the moment, but no doubt it is on file.
Was there any request from the municipality?
No.
Is there any income?

The hon. member for Richmond informs me that Mr. Malcolm
gave the public free use of the wharf while he was in business.
Port Maitland breakwater, $2,000.
This is to complete the reinforcing block of creosoted timber on the outer face and partial renewal of the flooring.
How long is it since the work was begun?
In 1908. The total estimated cost is $6,700, and this $2,000 is intended to complete the work.	-
Is this in Hants?
No, Yarmouth.
Has the work been done by contract?
No, by day labour.
Is that the principle upon which the department proceeds in works of this kind?

The total work in any one year did not amount to more than $3,000, and it was considered by the engineer better to do it by day work. It was repairing work and, while that class of work can sometimes be done by contract, it is not always so.

Is this Mr. Perry, the
foreman, one of the faithful?
Does the hon member wish to ask if he is a faithful workman? I think he is.

Mr. Perry belongs to one of the oldest Tory families1 in the county of Yarmouth. I may say that it would be impossible to have that work done by contract. The breakwater came near being washed away last winter. The work is the tearing down of old work and building new.

I did not intend to raise talk over this matter, but I know that in the county I have the honour to represent the only people appointed on these jobs are the faithful. Occasionally, a man on our side gets a position by promising to help my opponent.

I do not hesitate to say that, so far as the foremen are concerned, if, in any locality, we can get a competent reliable man who is a Liberal I think it is our duty to appoint him. For, a Liberal is interested in doing satisfactory work, work that will be creditable to the government; a Conservative would be interested rather the other way-in work that will bring discredit upon the government. So far as men under the foremen are concerned, let him employ good workmen whatever their politics may be.
Are there no good Liberals at this place to be recommended?

If the hon. member (Mr. Blain) heard what I said, he will know that I stated that this gentleman belonged to one of the oldest Tory families in the county. But I wish to add that he has seen the light.

That is the explanation.
By whose recommendation was the gentleman appointed and what were his special qualifications for the position?
He was appointed by my direction.
Further, the resident engineer, Mr. Dodwell, has told me several times lately that Mr. Perry was one of the best foreman he had had for men in the province of Nova Scotia.
At whose recommendation was he appointed?

I do not carry in my head the names of those who make such representations. I have no doubt that I satisfied jnyself that Mr. Perry was a thoroughly competent man. And I may say also that it is one of the instructions to the resident engineer that when a foreman is recommended he must satisfy himself of the competency of that foreman.

I suppose we shall have to agree with the minister that, when a position is open, a Liberal must get it. But I would ask him to instruct his resident engineer and director to occasionally give a ,T(?ry a ]ob' if is notbing better than as a labourer. In my county, a Tory cannot get even day's work on one of these government jobs.
I think the labourers are employed irrespective of party.

In my county, our Liberal friends go at these things as though it were their own money and we had nothing to do with it. I don't see why a poor Tory might not have a chance occasionally. You might kindly make a note of that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Was it the practice to give the poor Liberals a show in former years?
Always.
I have only been in politics a short time, I am a mere lamb in politics, but I understand the Liberals did get a job occasionally. If I remember, one or two Liberals were appointed to the Senate.
It might be a good idea for the hon. gentleman to send some of that advice up to the government at Toronto.
Was there a subforeman on this work as well as a foreman?
An assistant foreman.
How many men were employed?
I cannot give that information, I have no memorandum as to that.
Was there also an inspector?
The work would be inspected by the resident engineer, Mr. Dodwell, of Halifax.
Is the resident engineer always relied on to inspect the work?
The foreman is relied on first of all to see that the work is well done, but the engineer is relied on to visit the work from time to time to see that it is done properly.
I see that in the majority of cases of construction of wharfs and breakwaters there is an inspector.
That is where the work is being done under contract.
Only where it is under contract?
Done under contract.
Is that the practice?
Unless you call the foreman an inspector.
What is the foreman's duty?

The foreman is in charge. It is his duty to see, where the work is done by the day, that it is done according to the plans and specifications. We do not have an inspector where work is being done by the day, in addition to the foreman, but where it is done under contract we have an inspector.
As a matter of fact, those are the chief duties of a foreman, to inspect the work. Does he engage the workmen?
He employs them.
And purchases the materials?
He purchases the materials and sees that the work is done.
What are the duties of the subforeman?
To assist the foreman. He is really more like the head labourer.
But the foreman does not take any part in the work, he supervises it.
Oh, yes, the foreman, if he is a good man, very often takes off his coat and works with the rest.

The minister was very kind in stating that wherever there was a Qualified Liberal available he preferred to have him appointed to the supervision of work of this character. Does he think it is good policy that these men, good Liberals as they are, where they are so appointed, should discriminate between Liberals and Conservatives when it conies to engaging a labourer on this work? I mean that a man should he asked his political leanings, how he is going to vote, in order to determine whether or not he is entitled to labour on that government work.

The foremen are left free, so far as it has ever come under my observation, to employ such labouring men as in their judgment are best qualified to do the work. The government has never interfered in connection with the politics of a labouring man. The foreman is left free to exercise his good judgment, to get good workmen at fair wages, and to see that they do their work properly.

Would the minister approve of such a policy? It has been the practice for them to ask workmen how they were going to vote before they were engaged. When the answer came: I am not going to vote Liberal, the men were turned away. I do not suppose the minister is aware that that position exists to-day in Nova Scotia.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think it would be highly improper that a man should be asked how he is going to vote, that he should be asked to make any promise as to his vote in connection with his employment. The first consideration should be to get good capable men and it generally happens that men are found in both political parties for work of that character. But suppose there is a limited number of men required, what harm would there be if a preference were given to the friends of the government? I do not think we should have any hypocrisy in this matter. I propose every time, all other things being equal, to give a preference to my friend in every relation of life. What is wrong with it?

We have heard the hon. gentleman express that opinion many times in the House but when it comes to employing labourers in work of this kind I am surprised that the minister should make such a statement. It is not the government's money.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I did not say it was.

It is the money of the people of this country and surely if a man happens to be a Conservative, he has
been taxed for that money and why has he not a perfect right to participate in that work?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not see any distinction in respect to the labouring man and the man who might be a candidate for the highest office in the country. Our system of government is a party system. With all its faults it is the best that has been discovered. It is the British system and a preference is given by the government wherever the party system prevails to its own friends. There is nothing wrong in that. It would be perfect hypocrisy to pretend that the Conservative party did not practice that during the whole 18 years they were in power. My hon. friend from Colchester (Mr. Stanfield) says he is only a lamb. He is old enough to know that in his own county that rule was thoroughly enforced, he knows that a man could not get employment on the Intercolonial railway in the days of the Conservative administration unless he was identified with the Conservative party, and we did not kick about it either, we recognized it and we did not squeal. When these hon. gentlemen opposite talk about the poor Tory not getting any chance, I wish they had a l'ittle of that compassion for the poor Liberal in the olden days.
I simply wished to remind the minister that this was not his money.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I did not say it was our money. It is the money of the people of Canada, but the government of Canada are the custodians of that money and they are answerable to the people of Canada for the way in which they expend it. If it is a crime to give a preference to a Liberal the government will have to be turned out for that crime.

The Minister of Finance has been very frank in his statement to the committee. His frankness deserves that I should be equally candid. He has stated that he considers it perfectly proper that a man should be asked his politics.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, I did not say that. I said I would regard it as highly improper that when a man comes to work he should be asked anything about his politics. In every small community in Canada every man's politics is thoroughly well known, and I say that if a preference was given by the government of the day, be it Liberal or Conservative, to its own friends, always with the condition that they are capable, good men, I do not think there is anything to complain of. No one is hurt, the public interest does not suffer so long as the work is done properly. It can be as well done by a good Liberal as by a good Tory. What is the difference?
The minister stated that in the good old times the poor Liberals did not get any share.
They were not the good old times, say the old times.

Well, call it any kind of a time you like. Now, he says that he considers that in every district in Canada it is unnecessary to ask a man's politics because the politics of the people are generally pretty well known. I am going to say, with regard to the work which was done at Digby during the election of 1908, that men who went to the government pier to make application for work were asked: How are you going to vote?-and if they said that they were not going to vote Liberal, as many of them frankly did, they were told that they could not get any work, that they were bleu. Consequently they were not permitted to share in the labour which was available. The minister has said that in the good old days the poor Liberals did not get an opportunity to share in any of this labour or to receive any benefit from it. On that same public wharf at Digby, when money was expended under the Conservative regime, Liberals and Conservatives indiscriminately were given and had equal opportunities for employment. That is a matter of fact and it is a matter of record which the minister, I dare say, can verify if he chooses to look up the returns in the department, because, as he says, the poltical leanings of the people are so well known in these -different districts. I am not finding any fault. The minister does not, I hope, think that I am one of those who squeal, as he has expressed it, because I do not squeal ; I merely ask that every person in the community, without regard to his political qualifications, be permitted to share in this work.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not say that I would approve of what the hon. gentleman says occurred at Digby. If it is a fact that men came and asked for work and were told that they could not get it unless they voted in a certain way I certainly would not approve of it, and, while I am bound to accept my hon. friend's statement, I would be very much surprised if it occurred.
I can assure my hon. friend that it did occur.
The minister would dispose of that fact by the statement that those in charge of these works were not thoroughly versed in the politics of the people.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would assume that as a rule they do know.
They do know what their politics are?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As a rule they do know. I may say to my hon. friend that they are well informed people in Nova Scotia and as a rule in any of the small districts the average man knows the politics of his neighbour. If a preference were given to men who were friends of the government, always provided they were good men, nobody would be hurt.
What do you suppose would happen if we appointed a good Tory foreman?
I presume he would do about the same as anybody else.
He would employ Tory labourers.

Perhaps he would. If he did I would say he would not be doing right. But I do not deny that the Minister of Public Works or any other minister has the right to employ anybody else than his own friends in Dositions of trust. Perhaps that is a fair proposition, but I am simply speaking of the labourers. This is public monev and let the people have the money. There are always men who are particular to say that they are a great help to the party when sometimes they are not much of a help after all. All I plead for is that the ordinary workman shall be given a fair show and that he shall not be handicapped on account of his politics.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I should be surprised if it could be shown in the case of any work requiring any considerable number of labourers that the men were all of one political faith. It has generally happened in cases that have come under my observation that men of both parties have been employed. It generally happens that if you want a good many men you have to take men at certain seasons because you cannot get them at other seasons. My observation is that as a rule there are men of both political parties employed. My hon. friend seems to think that it is a great crime for a member of parliament or a prominent Liberal to give a recommendation to anybody to get employment. I cannot quite see-it in that light. I have no doubt that every member in this House is in the habit of getting a recommendation from some one asking him to be good enough to do something to help somebody. What is wrong in that?

It is perfectly proper to give a man a recommendation, but what I
complain of is that the rule was made that a man could not get work unless he was recommended by a Liberal.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman was good enough to say that he has heard me many a time in Halifax express my gratitude to good Conservatives. That is true, but don't make any mistake about it, I never had anything to thank the Conservative party machine for. I never ran an election in Nova Scotia that I did not have to fight the whole Conservative party machine for what is was worth. I never owed them anything, but I do owe much to high-minded independent Conservatives who were good enough to vote for me and I have always been ready to express my indebtedness to them. I never ran an election for the local legislature that I was not opposed by every power the federal government could bring to bear against me.

The conditions must be very different in Nova Scotia from what they are in Ontario if opponents of the Nova Scotia government are employed on public works. In my riding of West Kent, where the federal government has very kindly given an appropriation for public works, we have Mr. Fluke, a Liberal contractor, doing the work, and at the last elections he had eight or ten men in his employment who were nearly all Conservatives. We also had another contract where a Conservative was the contractor and he had many Conservatives working for him drawing the money which was appropriated by this government. If the Conservatives have any grievance in Nova Scotia they certainly have not in the other provinces.
Was that contract let after public competition, or is the work being done by day work?

The work was let after public competition and Mr. Fluke was the contractor and the men working on the job were nearly all Conservatives. I can assure you that as far as myriding is! concerned the Conservatives are not discriminated against. They have the same chance of getting work as the Liberals have, and I only wish the Conservative government in Toronto would be as generous to the Liberals as the Liberal government here is to the Conservatives.
I am glad to hear the hon. gentleman compliment the Conservative government of Toronto on the policy they adopt of letting public works by open competition.

I did not say anything about that. I merely expressed the hope that the Ontario government would be as willing to give employment to Liberals as the Liberal government here is to give employment to Conservatives on public works.

The policy of the Ontario government is to put everything possible up to public competition but the hon. gentleman (Mr. McCoig) was a member of the Ontario legislature and he supported a government which did not carry out that kind of a policy.
No.
Take for instance the policy of the Boss government with regard to the school books.
Is the question of the Ontario school books before the Chair?

I desire to correct the hon. gentleman. The Minister of Finance advocates the employment on public works of the party friends of the government, and he says that is the British system. The minister takes steps to give these things good appearance. But the result was that the Maritime Dredging Company and Mr. John E. Moore, the minister's friend, received three or four times the value of the work. And the Auditor .General's Report, which I have consulted, shows that the inspection charges require investigation. About $600 or $700 was spent for inspection on this work. There were three or four inspectors, one at $5 a day, one at $3, and another at $2.50, and my recollection is that they had seventy or eighty days more than the time within which the work was in progress. These inspectors are appointed by the ministers, and I have not the slightest doubt appointed upon the recommendation of the contractor. .

Unless the hon. member has information to that effect, he ought not to make that statement. I tell him that there is no foundation whatever for the statement. No inspector in New Brunswick or elsewhere is put on at the recommendation of the contractor. The hon. member ought to know that he should have the most positive evidence before making a statement of that kind.

Notwithstanding the minister's statement, I have no hesitation in expressing my opinion that, in the dredging that goes on in New Brunswick, the inspectors are in league with the contractors. What does the hon. minister think
of the dredging at Dalhousie and the inspection certificates put through in that case? It developed in court that the dredging inspection was done and the records kept by an employee of the firm of A. & R. Loggie, who sued the inspector, issuing a summons against him in the magistrate's court. And the matter was fixed up. Does the minister mean to say that Mr. Alleyne, the dredging inspector, was thoroughly independent of the firm of A. & R. Loggie, or that the Inspection was done without reference to the interests of the firm? It is very well for the minister to make such statements as that which he has made, but it has been and will be pretty difficult to make the people in communities where the dredging is done believe that fraud is not being committed on the public treasury in connection with these dredging contracts in different parts of the country. It is only necessary to examine the certificates and note the handwriting of some of these inspectors. They are men who write with the greatest difficulty and could not possibly figure a cube. Such things are reported to me from different parts of the country. I have no hesitation in expressing my belief that these dredging grafts are worked in many cases by dishonest and fraudulent inspection. So, I think that when the minister comes down with an estimate of this kind for dredging, the House _ is entitled to have information as to just how that money is to be expended-whether it is to be expended by contract given out in this way or upon dredges owned by the government. It seems_ to me that there is a great deal of dredging done and let by contract to private contractors that ought to be done by the government dredges. The government own a very extensive dredging plant and I thought it was the intention that as much dredging as possible should be done by the dredges owned by the government. There is no doubt that men have gone into this dredging business who had no experience and have gone into it to make money out of it relying on their political puil with the _ department and with the government. Since _my hon. friend became Minister of Public Works the firm of A. & R. Loggie has embarked upon that business with very profitable results to them. They have not been in the business very long but they have contracts to the extent of thousands of dollars. That firm is composed of gentlemen who have been very close to the Minister of Public Works.
Close in what way?
Politically and in every other way.
In what other way?
In every other way
What does the hon. gentleman mean now, ' in every other way.'
I say they were close friends and closely associated with the Minister of Public Works.
In what way?

The minister regards A. and R. Loggie as among his closest friends in the province of New Brunswick. Then there is the McAvity and the John E. Moore interest, who have also formed a dredging- company. They are ^ also very close to the Minister of Public Works, and I think when we see the thousands and thousands of dollars going to these firms, we should scrutinize these dredging contracts closely. I have no desire to make any reflections on any of these gentlemen, I am not here for that purpose. Any reflections I make are upon the department for allowing these things to take place. I have no hesitation in criticising them as wasteful expenditures. Dredging could be done in some cases for one-quarter or one-fifth of what has been paid by this government.

The hon. gentleman said that there was fraudulent dealing in connection with the dredging. There can be nothing fraudulent unless the contractor is guilty of fraud. How does the hon. gentleman reconcile that statement with his other statement that he makes no reflection on the contractors? If there is fraud, the contractors must be a party to it, and I cannot imagine a more serious charge for a member to make than to allege that the contractors have conspired together with the inspectors to send in fraudulent returns and so defraud the government. Let me say to my hon. friend that if he has information of that character, if he has information which would justify him as a public man in making that statement behind the backs of these contractors and sending it broadcast throughout this country, giving to it all the authority and weight that should be attached to the statement of a respectable and honourable member of this parliament, then he is negligent in his duty as a public man if he fails to give the necessary information to the officers of my department or to the officers of the Department of Justice in the province from which he comes, so that they may take the necessary proceedings in order to prevent any further defrauding of the public revenue, and to punish those whom he believes guilty of fraud. That is the duty the hon. member owes to himself, to parliament and the people whom he represents. Let me say to my hon. friend that he should be careful and take warning by the fate that has befallen some gentlemen who have preceded him in this parliament. I remember that an hon. member representing one of the Simcoes was in the habit of rising in his place in this parliament and making simi-Mr. PUGSLEY
lar accusations with regard to the treasury being defrauded by dredging contracts. He was never able to prove the assertions he made and when he went back, to his people where a considerable amount of this dredging was being carried on and where he had alleged fraudulent transactions were going on from week to week and from month to month, the people of the constituency let that hon. gentleman know what they thought of the exaggerated accusations he had so often made in this House. Let me say to my hon. friend that as one occupying a seat in a parliament of gentlemen he ought not to make these accusations unless he is prepared to back them up and give the proof of the statements he makes.
In regard to A. and R. Loggie, I do not know whether they went into the dredging business after I became minister or not. I think they were in the business before I became minister, in fact I am satisfied they were, and my deputy so informs me. Let me say further that they are not intimate personal friends of mine, I do not know whether I can say they are active political friends. I think that they but seldom take an active part in politics. They are men who stand in the veTy front rank of merchants and manufacturers in the Dominion of Canada. They are men who by patience and energy and devotion to their business have built up a very large business which extends over various parts of the provinces of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, and I think it extends up into the province of Quebec. Until to-night I have never heard any insinuations thrown out against their integrity. The hon. gentleman has chosen to insinuate that they have gone into the dredging business because they are friends of the Minister of Public Works, and he throws out the insinuation that they hope in some way by reason of that fact to secure benefits at the expense of the treasury of this country. Let me say that, so far as I know, since I became minister the Messrs. Loggie have never secured a single contract except by public competition when they were the lowest tenderers, and I know of no misconduct on the part of inspectors, I know of no misconduct or wrong doing on the part of Messrs. Loggie, and I have yet to learn that it is any crime for any man in this country to tender for a public work. I have yet to learn that it is any crime on the part of the minister to award a contract for any public work to the man who happens to be the lowest tenderer, even although he may belong to the same political party as the minister.
With regard to Messrs. Moore and McAvity it is true they are engaged in the dredging business, but they are both men of large activities, they are men who en-

gage in many lines of business, they are active, energetic, enterprising men. One of them Mr. Moore, is the president of the Maritime Dredging Company. What connection Mr. McAvity has with the company I do not know, but whether he has any connection or not makes no difference. Let me say that the contract for dredging both upon the St. John river and Maqua-pit lake and the harbour of St. John were let to the Maritime Dredging Company after public competition and after everybody had had full and fair opportunity of tendering for the work.
And after they had '_een put to work on the job.

I do not remember whether they were on the work, but if so it was distinctly under this agreement that the work should be let by public tender and that for any work which they did in the meantime, pending the awarding of the contracts, the Maritime Dredging Company were to receive the price at which the work was tendered for by the lowest tenderer. Bu't no assurance was given them and they had no expectation that they would receive the contract unless they happened to be the lowest tenderers. Tenders were advertised for in the leading daily newspapers of St. John and everybody had an opportunity of tendering for this work. Take the case that my hon. friend spoke of. The hon. gentleman says that it is well known that the money is being wasted and that the contractors are receiving amounts larger than they aTe entitled to. Upon what does my hon. friend base that statement?
I did not say that in reference to the St. John Harbour contract.
Then, my hon. friend, I understand, limits his charge to the Ma-quapit lake work.
That and the payment of 90 cents per cubic yard to the Maritime Dredging Company for the Gasperaux river work.

I will deal first with the Maquapit lake work. This is out of order and I would not have referred to it but for the extraordinary statement of the hon. gentleman. As to the Maquapit lake work, my hon. friend ought to know that dredging in different places does not always cost the same amount of money. A good deal depends upon the extent of the work that is to be done. Then, the question of the cost of a dredge enters into the calculation of the contractor. A good deal depends upon the nature of the soil which has to be excavated. But it so happens that all these considerations were taken into account, I presume, by the contractors who tendered for this work at 50 cents per cubic yard.
My chief engineer, who has had a large experience in these matters and who had the report of the resident engineer before him, certified that the price was fair and reasonable and the contract was awarded to the Maritime Dredging Company.
Now, let me speak of the work which my hon. friend referred to at the Gasperaux river. Tenders were called for the work. I am not quite sure whether there was any tender put in except that of the Maritime Dredging Company. The work was very widely advertised but there were very few people, if any, outside that company who. were willing to undertake it. The work is at a very exposed place, at Port Elgin- whether it is upon the straits of Northumberland or not I do not remember at this moment-and the cost of towing the dredge there was very large. There was a great deal of danger connected with it. While the work of dredging was going on one of the scows was wrecked involving a very large loss to the contractors. Although the Maritime Dredging Company were offered the work for the next season at the same price of 90 cents per cubic yard, they refused to again enter into a contract and declined to go back there last spring. In consequence of that we were obliged to wait for a number of months before we could make any arrangements for doing the work, and, being unable to get them to send their dredge back, we were obliged, late in the fall, to undertake the continuance of that work by means of the government dredge which we brought from Nova Scotia.
Now then, in face of these facts, how can the hon. gentleman expect this committee to believe there was anything wrong in the awarding of that contract to the Maritime Dredging Company? The only other contract to which reference has been made is that in the city of St. John. What took place there? You have the right to look at. all the work which this company is doing. Before I became Minister of Public Works my predecessor, having invited tenders by public competition, received tenders for this work and the lowest tender received was 90 cents per cubic yard. When I became minister, recognizing the necessity of continuing that work, I asked myself how it would be possible to get the work done at a lower price? In past years the practice had been to let contracts from year to year. I determined that I would let a contract extending over a number of years because I thought that in that case there would be an encouragement to the contractors to purchase a dredge and that they would be willing, as they would be sure of the work extending over a number of years, to tender at a lower price than they would be if they only had the contract for one year. I called for tenders and the result was that the Maritime Dredging Company tendered for the work at 39 cents per cubic



yard, a little more than one-third of what had been previously paid for dredging in St. John harbour. The hon. gentleman referred to the dredging work that Mr. Mayes did at one time at 55 cents per cubic yard, and afterwards at 90 cents per cubic yard. We are getting the dredging done, and a very important work it is, in the harbour of St. John, by the Maritime Dredging Company at either 39 or 39J cents per cubic yard.
Just a word in regard to the inspectors. 1 say to my hon. friend that in no single case has an inspector been appointed who was supposed to have any relations of any kind or description with the contractors. So far, I know of no inspector having been appointed upon the recommendation of the contractors, and we have always been careful to see that they have no connection of any kind or description with the contractors so that they would not be likely to be in the slightest degree influenced in favour of the contractors. We have endeavoured to get honest men, and I believe we have honest men. I believe we have honest men in the employ of the government to-day as dredge inspectors, and until I have some better evidence than the mere statement of my hon. friend that these inspectors are dishonest, I shall continue to believe that they are honest. I shall continue to believe they are honest until I have evidence to the contrary.
I	would say to my hon. friend that I think the fair thing for him to do would be to investigate these accounts thoroughly. 1 have no objection to the most thorough investigation before the Public Accounts Committee, but I do say to him that in all fairness to those who are not here to defend themselves he ought not to be throwing out these insinuations unless he has the facts to support such statements, and if he has the facts to support them, then it is his duty to submit these facts to the proper officers of the Crown whose duty it is to take criminal proceedings and give them an opportunity of taking such a course as they may deem to be best in the public interest. The hon. gentleman has now the opportunity of going to his own political friends. It so happens that the Premier of New Brunswick, who is also the Attorney General of that province, is a political friend of the hon. member who represents the county of York and who has made these insinuations. I have no doubt that if he goes, in the discharge of his duty, and submits the facts to the Attorney General he will feel it to be his duty to take the necessary steps in order to punish those who have defrauded the treasury of this country, if there has been any defrauding of the treasury, although I do not hesitate to tell the committee that I do not believe it, and I shall refuse to believe it Mr -PUGSLEY.
until I have some positive evidence that there has been such fraud as my hon. friend insinuates.

I think I have a full sense of my responsibilities and duties as a member of this House, and that I do not require any instructions from the Minister of Public Works in that behalf. I stated that I believed in many cases in connection with dredging contracts in New Brunswick the public treasury had been defrauded of large sums of money. I stated that and I reiterate that now as my firm belief. I say this after having investigated, to some extent, the accounts in connection with the dredging operations and after having had communicated to me information by letter and by personal interview by several very reliable men in different parts of New Brunswick. I referred to one case, the contract of A. and R. Loggie for dredging at Dalhousie. I state what is my absolute and firm belief founded on information communicated to me by persons of unquestioned reliability. I have a letter from Dalhousie stating that Mr. Alleyne who was appointed-and I have since discovered that he was appointed upon the order of the Minister of Public Works to do the inspecting at that place-has been paid day after day during the whole season, and that for many days he was not there at all. There is a memorandum upon the file signed by the Minister of Public Works asking that this same Mr. Alleyne be appointed. He was appointed, but the work was done by another person, and my information is that he wa's an employee of the firm of A. and R. Loggie and that a summons was issued in the magistrate's court.
Issued by whom?
Issued by the man who did the inspecting.
Against whom?

Against the inspector who was receiving the money from the government. That is my information, and when the summons was issued and served it was fixed up through the intervention of the contractor. As . to .the dredging of Maquapit lake this was the easiest sort of dredging, dredging a channel where there was three feet of water to the depth of seven, feet. The minister has said that there has been no case in which a contract has been let to the firm of A. & R. Loggie, and I think he added, or to any other firm in New Brunswick, without a tender. What has the Minister of Public Works to say as to this? I hold in my hand a copy of a telegram which reads:
Dalhousie, Oct. If, 1908. Eugene D. Lafleur, Ottawa.
Kindly authorize resident engineer Stead to put dredge ' Hayward ' at work at Bathurst

at same price as Caraquet contract, to be certified fair and reasonable by Mr. Stead, work not to exceed $5,000.
Signed, WM. PUGSLEY.
What is the date?
The 14th October at Dalhousie, when the minister was down there in the election campaign and after no doubt he had seen his friend, Mr. Loggie.
Was that to be at the same rate as the other?

Prices to be certified fair and reasonable by Mr. Stead. Well, I have had occasion to look into some of Mr. Stead's certificates and to judge of the value of his certificates as to what is fair and reasonable, and perhaps when we come to some other matters that have occurred in, the province of New Brunswick this House will have more light as to the value to be attached to any certificate furnished by Mr. Stead as to fairness and reasonableness. But there is the telegram signed by the minister himself telegraphing from Dalhousie, where Mr. Loggie was, to his engineer and instructing him to give Loggie's dredge this work at prices to be fixed by the minister's engineer, Mr. Stead. I think, Mr. Chairman, that the people of the province of New Brunswick, where this work is being done, will require something more than a display of affected indignation on the part of the Minister of Public Works. He invariably shields himself-that has been his habit for many years-when a statement is made which reflects upon himself or his department by trying to treat it as something said against somebody else, and then he proceeds to laud that somebody else to the skies and to speak of him as some one of the highest reputation for honour and integrity and righteousness in which he is excelled by no man in the Dominion of Can-'ada. He has said that of his friend, Mr. McAvity, he has said that of his friend, Mr. Loggie. Well, these are private contractors and I am not here to criticise them,' but to criticise the Department of Public Works which is the trustee and servant of the people for not properly guarding the people's interests.
Does the hon. gentlemen say that a contractor has conspired with an inspector to defraud the department and yet makes no reflection on him?
What I said was that I was not here for the purpose of making reflections on these people who were dealing with the department, but my criticism is directed against the department.
Why do you do it then?

Because I am here as a representative of the people to criticise
the conduct of the department. I have no hesitation in saying that my firm belief is that there has been fraud in this connection and that the country is paying as much as fifty per cent and one hundred per cent in same cases for dredging above fair and honest prices.
Does the hon. gentleman suggest to this committee that there can be fraud unless the inspector and the contractor are parties to that fraud?

I am not saying whether that is so or not, but I do say and the great majority of the people in the communities who know what is going on, believe it, that these certificates upon which payment is being made to these very contractors are certificates which cannot be relied upon. I have referred to the certificate of Mr. Alleyne, appointed by the minister himself in connection with the Loggie contract; a certificate which has been brought down, and which would convince anybody that the man was not competent to estimate the quantity of dredging material worked by that firm or any other firm. In addition to that there is the information which has been communicated to me by a prominent resident of that community in reference to Mr. Alleyne's neglect of his duty, and the fact that it was known that he was not there day after day and for weeks at a time, but he signed these certificates upon statements prepared by another man who was in close relation with the Loggie firm. Now, Mr. Chairman, in view of these facts the House will be in a better position to properly judge the weight of the statement which the minister made, and as I say, it will require more than these exhibitions of affected indignation to which the minister always resorts when he claims that there are foul insinuations made against him or his friends; it will require more than his affected indignation to change the opinion of the residents of these communities where these things have gone on. So far as I am concerned it is not an insinuation. I state, as a member of this House, my firm belief, after examining the documents which have been brought down in connection with these contracts, and after having had communicated to me by reliable people these facts of which I have made mention.
The minister said he did not know whether this work would be done by contract or by the government dredge. Is there not a government dredge in that vicinity.
No.

Is there not one at Lunenburg?

Mr. PTKjSLEY. Not a government dredge; it belonged to the W. J. Poupore Company.
I understood there was a government dredge at Bridgewater not very long ago.

That was a Poupore dredge, but of course we have dredges at several places.
Yarmouth harbour improvements, $60,000.
This is to continue the very necessary work of improving the harbour at Yarmouth.
How is the dredging being done there?

It is done under contract. Tenders were called for, several were received, and the lowest tender was that of the Dominion Dredging Company, which is doing the work. The prices are 50 cents a yard for taking out to sea, and 30 cents to cast over.
How far do they have to take the material?
I have not that information.
About five miles.
What will be the total cost of the work?

That will depend on the extent of the improvement we shall make. We are widening and deepening the channel so as to accommodate the large steamers which now come to Yarmouth, especially those running to Boston. If we were to continue the. work to the full extent that would be useful the cost would run up to a large amount; but we do not think it necessary to do that. We can keep widening the channel gradually. At present we have in contemplation only the work for which we are now asking for an appropriation.
Will the work at Westport be done by contract?

Yes. The hon. member for Cumberland asked what the $367.77 was expended for at Diligent River harbour. It was for removing what is known as the Gore rock, which was a menace to navigation, about 225 tons of stone having been removed. Then, the hon. member for Digby asked me with regard to the wharf at Cen-treville. I may say that I have had a report made upon that wharf, and while it is a fairly useful work, I find that it will cost from $75,000 to $85,000. Therefore I am afraid that I cannot hold out much expectation that that work will be done in the near future.

I do not want the minister to confuse the repairs necessary to Mr. CEOSBY.
sustain the present structure with the very elaborate harbour improvement referred to in the report. The wharf at present there is liable to be carried away during any tempestuous weather and a comparatively small sum would retain that, and that is what I referred to.

The difficulty, in the opinion of the resident engineer is that it would be a waste of money to repair the present wharf, while to build a new one, which would be the only way to make it effective, would cost the sum I have stated.

All I can say is that it would be a most disastrous thing to allow that wharf to go down for the lack of a comparatively small sum of money. I know the wharf quite as well as the resident engineer. The entire business carried on there is dependent on that structure, and if it is allowed to go down, the business done there will be brought to an immediate termination, and many thousands of dollars invested in valuable plants will be entirely lost and hundreds of people thrown out of employment. So I hope the minister will either ask the resident engineer for a soecial report on that wharf, or send a special engineer to make a special report.

I cannot promise to
send a special engineer, but I will again look carefully into the report. My hon. friend also mentioned Battery Point, Digby, Nova Scotia. I find that a part of it belongs to the Department of Militia and Defence and the other part to the Dominion Atlantic Railway Company. Therefore, there is no obligation on my department to make any improvements.
